skillTips.vocabulary: Opposites help: trivial is defined by the large sum it stands against.
skillTips.detail: Match each payment size to its rating carefully, since the result runs against expectation.

passages.title: Paying For Play
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A reward looks like a pure addition. The child already enjoys drawing, so a prize for drawing should add to the enjoyment and produce even more drawing. In a much-cited study, the result went the other way. Children who were promised a certificate for drawing spent less free time drawing in a later session than children who drew for nothing, or who received the same certificate as a surprise afterward.

The standard account is called overjustification. Part of motivation is a story we tell ourselves about why we are doing something. Before the prize, the story is simple: I draw because I like it. After a promised prize, a second and louder explanation is available: I draw because someone rewards me. When the payment stops, the reason it replaced does not automatically return.

The effect has limits worth keeping in mind. It shows up mainly for activities people already find interesting, and mainly when the reward is expected and tied to the mere doing of the task. Rewards for genuine skill, or for work nobody would choose freely, behave quite differently.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Prizes always destroy a child's interest in art.
Children draw more when adults watch them closely.
Certificates are a poor way to record achievement.
An expected reward can replace a person's own reason for doing something they already enjoy, and interest drops when the reward stops.
questions.explanation: The study, the explanation, and the limits all describe a reward replacing the internal reason for an already enjoyed activity.

questions.stem: Which children spent the least free time drawing in the later session?
choices: Those promised a certificate before they drew.
Those who drew for nothing.
Those given the certificate as a surprise afterward.
Those who were asked not to draw.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph names the promised-certificate group as the one that drew less than either other group.

questions.stem: Based on the last paragraph, why would paying people for dull work they would never choose freely be less risky?
choices: Because dull work generally pays better.
Because the effect appears mainly with activities people already find interesting.
Because such workers do not notice rewards.
Because surprise rewards are impossible at work.
questions.explanation: There is no existing interest for the reward to replace, and the passage limits the effect to already interesting activities.

questions.stem: In this passage, mere means:
choices: carefully measured
shared with other people
nothing more than; only
repeated many times
questions.explanation: The mere doing of the task means simply doing it, as opposed to doing it well.

lesson.strategy: The passage begins with an assumption, reports a study that breaks it, names the explanation, then limits it. Read the last paragraph as a fence around the claim rather than a new idea. The word mainly appears twice there, and each time it narrows what the effect covers.

signals.phrase: In a much-cited study, the result went the other way
signals.means: The assumption just stated is contradicted by evidence.

signals.phrase: The standard account is called overjustification
signals.means: The explanation is being named; a definition follows.

signals.phrase: When the payment stops, the reason it replaced does not automatically return
signals.means: The mechanism of the whole effect, in one sentence.

signals.phrase: The effect has limits worth keeping in mind
signals.means: Conditions on the claim are coming; do not over-apply it.

vocab.inContext: a printed award given to mark an achievement
having a second, outside reason that pushes aside your own reason
the reason a person has for doing something
only, nothing more than that

skillTips.main-idea: The main idea must fit the limits paragraph too; a choice that says always is usually too strong.
skillTips.inference: Apply the stated conditions to a new case rather than guessing from experience.
skillTips.vocabulary: Long words often contain a smaller one; justification sits inside overjustification.
skillTips.detail: Three groups are compared here, so read the whole sentence before picking one.

passages.title: Blaming The Person
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
When a stranger cuts in front of you in traffic, the explanation arrives before the thought does: that driver is selfish. When you do the same thing, the explanation is different. You were late, the lane was closing, the sun was in your eyes. Psychologists call this asymmetry the fundamental attribution error, the habit of explaining other people by their character and ourselves by our circumstances.

Two things sustain it. The first is visibility. You can see the other driver, but you cannot see the meeting he is late for; the person is vivid and the situation is invisible. The second is information. About yourself you hold a long record of behavior across many situations, which makes any single act look like an exception. About a stranger, one act is the whole file.

The error is not a small social slip. Judgments about poverty, failure, and crime all rest on how much weight we give to character over circumstance. Correcting it does not require believing that character is a fiction. It requires only the discipline of asking, before you decide, what you cannot see from where you stand.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea?
choices: Drivers are more selfish than other people.
We explain others by their character and ourselves by our situation, and that asymmetry shapes larger judgments.
Traffic is the best setting for studying human behavior.
Character does not exist; only situations matter.
questions.explanation: The passage names the asymmetry, explains what keeps it alive, and extends it to judgments about poverty, failure, and crime.

questions.stem: What two things does the passage say keep the error going?
choices: Anger and tiredness.
Habit and language.
Visibility and information.
Speed and distance.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph labels them first, visibility, and second, information.

questions.stem: Why do we grant ourselves situational explanations more easily?
choices: Because we know we are better people than strangers are.
Because our own actions are protected by law.
Because we hold a long record of our own behavior, so a single act looks like an exception.
Because we forget our own mistakes very quickly.
questions.explanation: The information point says a stranger's single act is the whole file, while our own act sits inside a long record.

questions.stem: In this passage, vivid means:
choices: brightly colored
moving very fast
hard to explain
easy to notice and strongly present
questions.explanation: Vivid stands against invisible in the same sentence, so it means standing out clearly to the observer.

lesson.strategy: The passage opens with a paired example, a stranger and yourself doing the same act, then names the error, gives two causes, and widens to social judgment. Use the pairing to keep the two halves of the asymmetry straight. The last paragraph states what the writer is not claiming, which is often exactly where a careful reader is tested.

signals.phrase: the explanation arrives before the thought does
signals.means: The judgment is automatic rather than reasoned.

signals.phrase: Two things sustain it
signals.means: Two causes follow; hold both of them.

signals.phrase: the person is vivid and the situation is invisible
signals.means: The first cause compressed into a single image.

signals.phrase: The error is not a small social slip
signals.means: The stakes are being raised; a wider claim follows.

vocab.inContext: two sides treated by different rules, here others and ourselves
the conditions around an action, such as being late or blinded by sun
standing out clearly and easy to notice
a habit of effort you hold yourself to on purpose

skillTips.main-idea: A main idea must cover the last paragraph too; here that means the wider social judgments.
skillTips.inference: Use the two labeled causes as your evidence; the right answer restates one of them.
skillTips.vocabulary: Paired opposites in one sentence, like vivid and invisible, define each other.
skillTips.detail: Numbered structures such as The first and The second are the most likely detail targets.

passages.title: When Results Do Not Repeat
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Around 2011, psychology began to audit itself, and the audit did not go well. A large collaboration repeated one hundred published studies, using larger samples and the original methods where those could be obtained. Fewer than half produced a result that reached statistical significance the second time, and the effects that did survive were, on average, roughly half the size first reported.

The temptation is to read this as a story about fraud. It is mostly a story about incentives. Journals preferred surprising, tidy findings; careers were built on them; and a researcher holding many measures and a flexible analysis could, in complete sincerity, wander toward the version of the data that worked. Nobody has to lie for a research literature to fill with results that are true only of the sample that produced them.

The response has been unglamorous and largely structural: preregistering hypotheses before the data are collected, publishing methods that are accepted before any results exist, sharing raw data, and running samples large enough to detect the modest effects that human behavior actually offers. The irony is worth holding onto. A field that lost public trust by overstating what it knew has recovered some of it by publishing, in detail, the record of being wrong.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the argument of the passage?
choices: Psychology was found to rest mainly on deliberate fraud.
Repeating old studies is a waste of research money.
Many published findings failed to repeat, largely because of incentives and flexible analysis, and the field answered with structural reform.
Larger samples reliably produce larger effects.
questions.explanation: The passage rejects fraud as the main cause, names incentives instead, and devotes the last paragraph to structural fixes.

questions.stem: What happened to the effects that did survive the repeat attempts?
choices: They were on average about half the size first reported.
They doubled in size.
They disappeared completely.
They appeared only in the original journals.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph gives this figure directly, alongside the count that reached significance.

questions.stem: What is the irony the passage points to at the end?
choices: That the audit was carried out by the same journals that caused the problem.
That trust lost by overstating knowledge was partly regained by publishing a detailed record of error.
That preregistration makes surprising findings more common.
That the public never learned about the failures.
questions.explanation: The closing sentence sets losing trust through overstatement against recovering it through openly documented mistakes.

questions.stem: In this passage, sincerity means:
choices: the speed at which work is published
agreement between two researchers
honest belief, with no intention to mislead
the exact wording of a hypothesis
questions.explanation: The phrase in complete sincerity is what separates this behavior from the fraud the passage has just ruled out.

lesson.strategy: This passage reports a finding, rejects one explanation for it, offers another, and closes on an irony. The pivot is the pair of sentences about fraud and incentives: the easy reading is named so that it can be replaced. Read the last paragraph slowly, since the list of reforms runs through one long sentence and the final claim depends on holding that list in mind.

signals.phrase: the audit did not go well
signals.means: An understated summary of a bad result; the numbers follow.

signals.phrase: The temptation is to read this as a story about fraud
signals.means: A reading the writer intends to reject is being named.

signals.phrase: It is mostly a story about incentives
signals.means: The replacement explanation, stated flatly.

signals.phrase: The response has been unglamorous and largely structural
signals.means: The passage turns from diagnosis to remedy.

signals.phrase: The irony is worth holding onto
signals.means: The closing point is a reversal; read what follows with care.

vocab.inContext: a careful check of one's own work for errors
the rewards that quietly shape how people behave
genuine honest belief, without any intent to deceive
recording a prediction publicly before the data are collected

skillTips.main-idea: When a writer names a tempting explanation and rejects it, the main idea lives in the replacement.
skillTips.inference: Irony questions need both halves of the reversal; find what was lost and how it was regained.
skillTips.vocabulary: Read sincerity against fraud in the same paragraph; the contrast fixes its meaning.
skillTips.detail: Numbers here come in pairs, one for significance and one for effect size; do not swap them.

passages.title: The Last Bus Home
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Mira takes the last bus home every night. The bus comes at eleven. She works at a small hotel. She cleans the front desk before she leaves.

The driver is an old man named Bo. He knows her face. He waits two minutes when she is late. He never says why. He just looks at the door and holds the bus.

One night, Mira runs to the stop. She is very late. The bus is not there. She sits on the bench and feels tired. Then she sees lights. The bus comes back around the corner. Bo opens the door. "I went around the block," he says. "Two times." Mira gets in. She does not know the right words, so she only says thank you. Bo nods. The bus moves.

Outside, the shops are dark and the street is wet. Mira looks at the window. She can see her own face in the glass. She is smiling. It is a small thing, she thinks. A bus that waits. But a small thing can make a hard day feel light.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: Mira wants to find a new job closer to her home.
Bo is angry because Mira is late for the bus.
A small act of waiting from a bus driver changes how Mira feels about a hard day.
Buses in Mira's city are usually late at night.
questions.explanation: The last paragraph states the point directly: a small thing, like a bus that waits, can make a hard day feel light. The other choices are not in the text.

questions.stem: What time does the last bus come?
choices: At eleven.
At nine.
At ten.
At midnight.
questions.explanation: The second sentence says, "The bus comes at eleven."

questions.stem: Why does Bo drive around the block two times?
choices: He forgot the way to the hotel.
He is giving Mira more time to reach the stop.
He is looking for other passengers.
He wants to buy something before work ends.
questions.explanation: The text already says Bo waits two minutes when Mira is late. On this night she is very late, so driving around the block is another way of waiting for her.

questions.stem: In "Bo nods," the word nods means that Bo —
choices: shouts at her
opens the window
asks her for money
moves his head down and up to mean yes
questions.explanation: Mira says thank you and Bo answers without words. To nod is to move the head down and up to show yes or agreement.

lesson.strategy: This is a short story with a simple shape: a habit, one special night, then a feeling. Read the first paragraph for the normal routine, the middle for what is different this time, and the last paragraph for the meaning. The sentences are short, so read for the change, not for hard words.

signals.phrase: every night
signals.means: This is a habit, something that happens again and again — the normal situation.

signals.phrase: One night
signals.means: The story now moves to one special day. Something different is coming.

signals.phrase: Then she sees lights
signals.means: The turning point. The problem is about to be solved.

signals.phrase: It is a small thing, she thinks
signals.means: The writer is telling you the lesson of the story here.

vocab.inContext: a long seat, here at the bus stop
the group of streets around one square of buildings; driving around it means going in a circle and coming back
moves his head down and up to say yes

skillTips.main-idea: In a short story, the main idea is usually a feeling, not a fact. Ask: what changed for the character by the end?
skillTips.inference: The story does not say Bo waited on purpose. Use the earlier line about waiting two minutes to work it out.
skillTips.vocabulary: When you meet a new word, look at the action around it. Mira says thank you, so Bo's answer must be a friendly sign.
skillTips.detail: Numbers and times are easy to check. Go back and find the exact sentence instead of trusting memory.

passages.title: The Extra Loaf
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Teodor has run the bakery on Sedge Street for nineteen years. He counts his flour, his salt, and his orders. Then he bakes one loaf more than he needs. He does this because of a winter long ago, when a woman knocked after closing time. She had no money, and he had nothing left to sell. He remembers her face better than he remembers that whole year.

So now the extra loaf sits on the top shelf, wrapped in brown paper. Most days nobody comes for it, and Teodor gives it to the birds in the square. His nephew calls this waste. Teodor says it is not waste; it is a promise. The bread is not the point. The shelf is.

Once or twice a month, someone does come. A student. A man leaving a night shift. A mother with a stroller and no coins. Teodor never asks questions. He takes the loaf down, hands it over, and turns back to his oven while they are still saying thank you.

That way, he says, nobody has to look grateful. They can just eat.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the main idea?
choices: Teodor bakes better bread than the other bakers on his street.
Teodor keeps one spare loaf every day as a promise he made to himself after failing to help someone.
Teodor is losing money because he bakes more bread than he sells.
Teodor wants his nephew to take over the bakery.
questions.explanation: The story links the extra loaf to the winter night he had nothing to give, and Teodor himself calls it a promise. The other choices are details or ideas the text never states.

questions.stem: How long has Teodor run the bakery on Sedge Street?
choices: Nine years.
Ten years.
Nineteen years.
Ninety years.
questions.explanation: The first sentence says nineteen years.

questions.stem: Why does Teodor turn back to his oven while people are still thanking him?
choices: So they do not feel they owe him anything.
Because he is angry that they came so late.
Because the bread will burn if he waits.
So he can count how many loaves are left.
questions.explanation: The last line explains it: that way nobody has to look grateful, they can just eat. He steps away so the person is not forced to perform thanks.

questions.stem: As used in the passage, grateful means —
choices: hungry after a long day
poor and without money
angry at being helped
showing that you feel thankful to someone
questions.explanation: People are saying thank you, and Teodor does not want them to have to look grateful — that is, to show visible thanks.

lesson.strategy: This story explains a strange habit. The first paragraph shows the habit and the memory behind it, the second shows what the habit looks like today, and the last two give its purpose. When a character does something odd, read forward until you find a reason word or a memory — that is where the explanation lives.

signals.phrase: because of a winter long ago
signals.means: The cause is coming. This explains why he bakes the extra loaf.

signals.phrase: So now
signals.means: Result. The past reason turns into today's habit.

signals.phrase: His nephew calls this waste
signals.means: Another opinion appears. The writer will answer it in the next sentence.

signals.phrase: That way, he says
signals.means: He is explaining his purpose — the point of the whole story is here.

vocab.inContext: one whole shaped piece of baked bread
using something for no good result; the nephew thinks the spare bread is thrown away for nothing
a small wheeled seat for pushing a baby
showing thanks to someone who helped you

skillTips.main-idea: When a character explains his own action ('it is a promise'), that line is usually very close to the main idea.
skillTips.inference: To infer, ask what a small action protects. Turning away protects the other person's pride.
skillTips.vocabulary: Words about feelings are often explained by the action beside them. 'Saying thank you' sits right next to 'grateful'.
skillTips.detail: Watch for numbers that look similar — nineteen and ninety sound close but mean very different things.

passages.title: Eleven Seconds Of Floating
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Ndidi signed up for swimming lessons at forty-one. She was the oldest person in the pool by twenty years, and she knew it.

The first lesson was not about swimming. The teacher, a calm woman named Roos, asked her to lie back in the shallow water and do nothing. Ndidi could not do nothing. Her legs dropped. Her shoulders tightened. Water went up her nose, and she stood again, coughing. "You are trying to hold yourself up," Roos said. "The water already does that. Your job is to stop helping."

It took five weeks. Then, one Tuesday evening, Ndidi lay back, opened her arms, and felt the water take her weight. She stayed there for eleven seconds. She counted them.

She still cannot swim far. Her stroke is slow and her breathing is loud. But she remembers those eleven seconds whenever a hard problem makes her tighten up. Some things do not need more effort, she thinks. Some things need less.

questions.stem: What does Ndidi mainly learn in this story?
choices: That swimming lessons are cheaper for older adults.
That she should have started swimming when she was young.
That her teacher is stricter than she expected.
That some problems get easier when you try less, not more.
questions.explanation: The last two sentences state it: some things do not need more effort, some things need less. That is what floating taught her.

questions.stem: How long did it take Ndidi to float?
choices: One lesson.
Five weeks.
Eleven weeks.
Twenty years.
questions.explanation: The text says plainly, "It took five weeks." Eleven is the number of seconds she floated, not weeks.

questions.stem: Why does Roos ask Ndidi to lie back and do nothing in the first lesson?
choices: Because Ndidi must learn to trust the water before she can swim.
Because the pool is too crowded for real swimming.
Because Ndidi is too old to move quickly.
Because Roos wants to test how long she can hold her breath.
questions.explanation: Roos says the water already holds her up and her job is to stop helping. The lesson is about letting the water do the work — trusting it — before learning strokes.

questions.stem: In this passage, shallow water is water that is —
choices: very cold
moving quickly
not deep
dirty
questions.explanation: She can stand up in it when she starts coughing, so it is water that is not deep.

lesson.strategy: This is a story of a slow success. Watch three stages: the first failure, the teacher's advice, and the moment it finally works. The time words ('The first lesson', 'It took five weeks', 'Then, one Tuesday evening') carry you from one stage to the next.

signals.phrase: The first lesson was not about swimming.
signals.means: Surprise. The writer is telling you the real subject is something else.

signals.phrase: It took five weeks.
signals.means: Time passes. The struggle was long, which makes the success matter.

signals.phrase: Then, one Tuesday evening
signals.means: The moment of change is here.

signals.phrase: But she remembers
signals.means: The story turns from the pool to the rest of her life — the lesson is being applied.

vocab.inContext: not deep; she can stand up in it
became stiff and hard, the opposite of relaxed
the arm movement used to push through the water when swimming

skillTips.main-idea: In a story about learning, the main idea is the lesson the character carries away, not the skill itself.
skillTips.inference: Use the teacher's spoken words. Dialogue in a short story is almost always there to explain the point.
skillTips.vocabulary: Check what the character can physically do. She stands up, so the water cannot be deep.
skillTips.detail: The same story can hold several numbers. Match the number to its unit — weeks, seconds, or years.

passages.title: The Other Suitcase
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Hugo took the wrong suitcase from the airport belt. Both were grey. Both had a red ribbon on the handle. He noticed only when he opened it in his hotel room and found a wedding dress, folded in white paper.

There was no name tag. There was a phone number written inside the lid, in pencil, half rubbed away. Hugo copied the digits and guessed the last one. He tried nine numbers before a woman answered.

Her name was Salla. She was getting married on Saturday, in a town two hours north, and she had spent the whole afternoon crying in a taxi. When Hugo said the words "white paper," she went quiet for a long moment. They met at the train station the next morning and traded bags. Salla tried to give him money. Hugo refused. He asked instead for a photograph after the wedding, so that he could see the dress on the right person.

Three weeks later, a small envelope reached his office. There was no letter inside, only a picture. Salla was laughing. The red ribbon from the suitcase was tied around her wrist.

questions.stem: What is the story mainly about?
choices: How airports lose luggage every day.
A stranger takes trouble to return something important, and asks for nothing.
A wedding that had to be cancelled.
Two travellers who become business partners.
questions.explanation: Hugo makes nine calls, meets Salla, and refuses money. The story is about the effort he makes for a stranger.

questions.stem: How did Hugo find Salla?
choices: He read a name tag on the handle.
The airport called her for him.
He found her address in the hotel.
He guessed the last digit of a pencilled phone number and called until she answered.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the number was half rubbed away, so he guessed the last digit and tried nine numbers before she answered.

questions.stem: Why does Salla go quiet when Hugo says the words "white paper"?
choices: She does not understand his language.
She is angry that he opened her bag.
Those words prove he really has her dress, and she is flooded with relief.
She thinks he is asking her for money.
questions.explanation: She had spent the afternoon crying over the lost dress. Only someone holding the bag would know it was folded in white paper, so his words prove the dress is safe.

questions.stem: In "they met at the train station the next morning and traded bags," traded means —
choices: gave each other the bag that belonged to the other person
sold the bags to a shop
carried the bags together
left the bags at the station
questions.explanation: Each of them had the other's suitcase, so trading means exchanging them so each got the right one back.

lesson.strategy: This is a plot story told in order: mistake, search, meeting, ending. Read it as a chain of events and keep asking 'what does he do next?'. The final paragraph does not explain the feeling in words — it shows one small object instead, so read that image carefully.

signals.phrase: Both were grey.
signals.means: This explains how the mistake was possible. Look for reasons hidden in short sentences.

signals.phrase: He noticed only when
signals.means: Marks the exact moment the problem is discovered.

signals.phrase: He tried nine numbers before a woman answered.
signals.means: Shows effort. The number tells you how much trouble he took.

signals.phrase: Three weeks later
signals.means: A jump forward in time. The ending is coming.

vocab.inContext: the moving band at an airport that carries bags to the passengers
the top cover of the suitcase
the single numbers that make up a phone number
exchanged — each person handed over the bag that belonged to the other

skillTips.main-idea: Ask what the character chose to do when he could have done nothing. That choice is usually the main idea.
skillTips.inference: When a character goes silent, look at what was just said and what they had lost. Silence often means strong feeling.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the situation. Two people each holding the other's bag can only be doing one thing when they meet.
skillTips.detail: Steps in a process are easy to mix up. Reread the paragraph and follow the actions in order.

passages.title: Between Two And Four
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Every night between two and four, Aurelio hosts a radio show that almost nobody hears. The station gave him the shift because nothing happens in it. Truck drivers, hospital staff, bakers — that is his audience, and it suits him. People awake at that hour rarely want to be entertained. They want proof that someone else is up.

For eleven months, a caller named Beatrix rang in at exactly three. She never had a topic. She described the weather on her street, the sound of the freight trains, the cat that sat on the wall opposite. Aurelio began holding the last segment open for her, though he never said so on air.

Then, in March, the calls stopped. He waited three weeks before mentioning it. When he finally did, six listeners phoned to say that they had noticed too, and that each of them had assumed they were the only person listening.

Aurelio still leaves the segment open. He fills it with music if he must. But he has stopped thinking of the show as talking into the dark. A quiet room, he has decided, is not the same as an empty one.

questions.stem: Which statement best captures the main idea?
choices: A host who believed he broadcast to nobody discovers that quiet listeners were there all along.
A radio station is trying to cancel an unpopular night programme.
A caller and a host slowly become close friends and then meet in person.
Night work is harder on the body than day work.
questions.explanation: The show 'almost nobody hears', then six listeners reveal themselves, and Aurelio concludes a quiet room is not an empty one. That arc is the main idea.

questions.stem: When did Beatrix call the show?
choices: Every night at two.
Once a month at four.
At exactly three, for eleven months.
Only during March.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says that for eleven months she rang in at exactly three.

questions.stem: What did the six phone calls make Aurelio realise?
choices: That Beatrix had told her friends to call him.
That his listeners preferred music to talk.
That the station was checking whether he still had an audience.
That silent listeners had been there all along, each one thinking they were alone.
questions.explanation: The callers said they had noticed the missing calls and had each assumed they were the only listener. That is why he stops thinking of the show as talking into the dark.

questions.stem: In this passage, a segment is —
choices: a request from a listener
one part of the radio programme
a break for advertisements
the salary paid for a night shift
questions.explanation: He holds 'the last segment' for Beatrix and later 'fills it with music', so it must be a section of the show.

lesson.strategy: The passage moves from a general situation to one specific loss and then to a change of mind. Read paragraph one for the setting, paragraph two for the pattern, paragraph three for the break in the pattern, and the last two sentences for the meaning. The final line is a quiet conclusion, not a plot event.

signals.phrase: The station gave him the shift because nothing happens in it.
signals.means: Gives the reason for his situation, and sets up the low expectations the ending will overturn.

signals.phrase: For eleven months
signals.means: Establishes a routine. Long routines in stories exist to be broken.

signals.phrase: Then, in March, the calls stopped.
signals.means: The turning point of the passage.

signals.phrase: But he has stopped thinking of the show as talking into the dark.
signals.means: The character's belief has changed. This is where the meaning is stated.

vocab.inContext: the fixed block of working hours he is given, here two to four in the morning
the people who listen to his programme
one part of a radio show, here the last part
believed something without checking whether it was true

skillTips.main-idea: When a story ends with a character changing their belief, the main idea is the old belief plus the correction.
skillTips.inference: Combine two facts the writer keeps apart: nobody phoned before, and six phoned now. The gap between them is the inference.
skillTips.vocabulary: Track how a word is used twice. 'Segment' is held open and then filled, so it is a slot of time.
skillTips.detail: Numbers cluster in this text — two, four, eleven, three, six. Attach each one to its noun before you answer.

passages.title: The Bowls She Breaks
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Ilse makes bowls for a living, and she breaks about a third of them herself. Customers find this strange. The bowls she destroys look perfectly good to them — even in shape, smoothly glazed, strong enough to hold soup for a decade. She breaks them anyway, on the stone step behind the workshop, without ceremony.

Her reason is not perfectionism, though everyone assumes it is. A bowl leaves her hands and lasts fifty years. In that time it will be used by someone she will never meet, in a kitchen she cannot imagine. She cannot ask those people what they wanted. So the only standard available to her is her own, and she has learned that a standard she bends once stops working.

There is one exception, on a shelf above the kiln. It is a bowl with a crooked rim, made the week her father died. It is the worst thing she has produced since she was a student. She has been offered money for it twice, and both times she has said that it is not for sale.

questions.stem: What is the central point of the passage?
choices: Ilse destroys bowls because she cannot sell enough of them.
Handmade bowls are stronger than factory bowls.
Because Ilse can never ask her future buyers what they want, she must hold to one unbending standard of her own.
Ilse is training to become a better potter than her teachers.
questions.explanation: The middle paragraph gives exactly this chain: the buyer is unknown and unreachable, so her own standard is the only one available, and it cannot be bent.

questions.stem: About how many of her bowls does Ilse break?
choices: About one in three.
About half.
All of the glazed ones.
Only the cracked ones.
questions.explanation: The first sentence says she breaks about a third of them herself.

questions.stem: Why does Ilse keep the crooked bowl instead of breaking it?
choices: It is worth more money than her other work.
Its value to her is personal, not a matter of craft quality.
It was made by her father, not by her.
She plans to repair the rim later.
questions.explanation: She calls it the worst thing she has made, yet keeps it because it was made the week her father died. Its meaning comes from memory, not from quality.

questions.stem: In "There is one exception," the word exception means —
choices: a bowl made for a special customer
a mistake that must be corrected
an extra bowl kept for testing
a case that does not follow the usual rule
questions.explanation: Her rule is that flawed bowls get broken. This bowl is flawed and is not broken, so it is a case outside the rule.

lesson.strategy: The passage sets up a puzzle, explains it, then breaks its own rule. Paragraph one shows the odd behaviour, paragraph two gives the reasoning behind it, and paragraph three shows the single case that contradicts it. Read the last paragraph as a deliberate contrast, not as a mistake by the writer.

signals.phrase: Customers find this strange.
signals.means: Signals that the behaviour is a puzzle, and that an explanation is coming.

signals.phrase: Her reason is not perfectionism, though everyone assumes it is.
signals.means: The writer removes the easy explanation first, so you read the real one more carefully.

signals.phrase: So the only standard available to her is her own
signals.means: 'So' marks the conclusion of the argument — this is the load-bearing sentence.

signals.phrase: There is one exception
signals.means: A reversal. Everything after this contradicts the rule you just learned.

vocab.inContext: covered with a hard glassy coating, which makes the bowl smooth and waterproof
the level of quality she requires before she will sell something
the one case that does not follow her usual rule
the top edge of the bowl, here bent out of shape

skillTips.main-idea: When a writer says 'her reason is not X', the real reason follows immediately. Read that sentence twice.
skillTips.inference: An object can matter for a reason outside its stated purpose. Ask what happened in the character's life when it was made.
skillTips.vocabulary: Abstract words like 'standard' and 'exception' are defined by the behaviour around them, not by a dictionary line.
skillTips.detail: Fractions count as details. 'A third' is not 'half', and the text is precise about it.

passages.title: What The Room Sounds Like
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Sanne records rooms. Not conversations, not music — rooms. She places a microphone in the middle of a space, asks everyone to leave, and captures four minutes of nothing.

The recordings go to an archive that most people will never open. Still, she is careful. A kitchen at noon has a hum from the refrigerator and a faint tick from the pipes. A school hallway at night holds the buzz of the ceiling lights and, underneath, the traffic outside. No two rooms sound alike, and no room sounds like silence.

Her hardest job was a factory that was closing after ninety years. The owners wanted a record of it. She arrived on the final morning, set up in the main hall, and asked the remaining workers to step outside. They stood in the yard without talking, while a machine that none of them would ever run again cooled behind them.

When she played the file back, one of the welders said it sounded wrong. Too thin, he said. Sanne agreed with him. She had recorded the building, she told him, not the work — and the work was the part he was missing.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states what the passage is about?
choices: Sanne's equipment is not good enough for large buildings.
Sanne records empty rooms, and one job shows her that a room without its people is missing the thing that mattered.
Factories are much noisier places than kitchens or schools.
An archive is paying Sanne to document buildings before they are demolished.
questions.explanation: The first half explains her work; the factory scene delivers the point when the welder finds the recording thin because the work is missing.

questions.stem: How long is each of Sanne's recordings?
choices: Four seconds.
Ninety minutes.
Four minutes.
One full day.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says she captures four minutes of nothing. Ninety refers to the factory's years.

questions.stem: Why did the recording sound "thin" to the welder?
choices: It held only the empty building, without the machines and people that gave the place its real sound.
The microphone was placed too far from the wall.
The factory had already removed most of its equipment.
He had never listened to a recording before.
questions.explanation: Sanne agrees and explains it herself: she recorded the building, not the work, and the work is the part he was missing.

questions.stem: In "a faint tick from the pipes," faint means —
choices: sudden and sharp
repeated many times
coming from far below
weak and hard to hear
questions.explanation: She is recording rooms that seem empty of sound, so a faint tick is one that is quiet and barely noticeable.

lesson.strategy: The passage explains an unusual job, then tests it with one hard case. Read paragraphs one and two for what she does and why it is not really silence, then read the factory story as the moment her method meets its limit. The final exchange of dialogue carries the meaning.

signals.phrase: Not conversations, not music — rooms.
signals.means: Defines the job by ruling other things out. Negative definitions tell you what to expect.

signals.phrase: Still, she is careful.
signals.means: A small contrast: even though nobody may listen, the care matters.

signals.phrase: Her hardest job was
signals.means: Signals the main example of the passage. Everything important happens here.

signals.phrase: one of the welders said it sounded wrong
signals.means: An objection. The writer uses it to reveal what the method cannot capture.

vocab.inContext: a stored collection of records kept for the future
a low, steady, continuous sound
weak and hard to hear
workers who join pieces of metal using heat

skillTips.main-idea: If a passage ends with a correction or a limit, the main idea usually includes that limit, not just the job description.
skillTips.inference: Take the character's own explanation seriously. Sanne states the reason, and the question only asks you to restate it accurately.
skillTips.vocabulary: Sound words are described by their neighbours: 'hum', 'tick' and 'buzz' are all small sounds inside an apparently empty room.
skillTips.detail: Two numbers here look alike — four minutes and ninety years. Match each number to its unit.

passages.title: The Village That Was Not There
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
In the third edition of his county atlas, Aurel Brenner drew a hamlet named Kessel where no hamlet stood. It was not a mistake. Mapmakers of his generation seeded their work with small inventions — a lane that led nowhere, a pond that had never held water — so that any rival who copied the plates would copy the lie as well, and convict himself.

What Brenner did not anticipate was the obedience of the world. A road crew, working from his atlas, cut a track toward Kessel because the atlas showed one. A cattle dealer raised a shed at the junction, reasoning that a hamlet with a road would soon want feed. Within a decade the shed had become a shop, the shop a post stop, and the post stop a cluster of nine houses whose residents, when asked, said they lived in Kessel.

Brenner visited once, late in life. He is said to have stood at the crossroads a long time without speaking. His trap had worked in reverse: instead of catching a thief, the invention had assembled a village, and the map, simply by being believed, had made itself accurate.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: A mapmaker who was punished for selling inaccurate atlases.
The technical difficulty of surveying a rural county.
A dishonest rival who stole an atlas and was taken to court.
A false place on a map that became a real place because people acted as though it existed.
questions.explanation: The final sentence states it: the map, by being believed, made itself accurate. The invented hamlet turned into a real settlement.

questions.stem: Why did mapmakers of Brenner's generation add invented features?
choices: To fill empty space on a crowded page.
To expose rivals who copied their maps.
To encourage new roads into empty country.
To hide places they had failed to survey.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says the invention existed so that a rival who copied the plates would copy the lie and convict himself.

questions.stem: Why does Brenner most likely stand silent at the crossroads?
choices: He is trying to remember which road leads home.
He is angry that a rival profited from his work.
He is facing the strange result that his own lie has become a true place.
He is disappointed that the village is smaller than he drew it.
questions.explanation: The passage calls it a trap that worked in reverse. He is standing inside a village that exists only because he invented it, and the text gives no evidence for the other readings.

questions.stem: In this passage, a hamlet is —
choices: a very small village
a paper map of a county
a crossroads with no buildings
a farm building for cattle
questions.explanation: Kessel grows from a shed to a shop to a cluster of nine houses whose residents say they live there, so a hamlet is a very small settlement.

lesson.strategy: This passage runs a causal chain: a deliberate lie, a series of ordinary decisions, and an unintended result. Read paragraph one for the intention, paragraph two for the chain of effects, and paragraph three for the irony. Each step in paragraph two causes the next, so follow the sequence shed, shop, post stop, houses.

signals.phrase: It was not a mistake.
signals.means: Blocks the obvious reading. The invented village was deliberate, and the reason follows.

signals.phrase: so that any rival who copied the plates would copy the lie as well
signals.means: States the original purpose — the standard against which the ending will be measured.

signals.phrase: What Brenner did not anticipate
signals.means: Warns you that the outcome will not match the intention. The consequence chain starts here.

signals.phrase: Within a decade
signals.means: Compresses time and marks the accumulation of small decisions into a large result.

signals.phrase: His trap had worked in reverse
signals.means: Names the irony directly: the mechanism produced the opposite of its purpose.

vocab.inContext: a very small village
to expect something before it happens
the world's readiness to do what the map told it, without questioning
to prove someone guilty; the copied lie would prove the rival had stolen the map

skillTips.main-idea: In an ironic story, the main idea is the distance between the intention and the outcome. State both halves.
skillTips.inference: When a character is silent, read the sentence that follows. The writer often explains the silence indirectly.
skillTips.vocabulary: Unknown nouns can be defined by what grows out of them: nine houses and residents tell you 'hamlet' means a tiny settlement.
skillTips.detail: Purpose questions ask why, not what. Find the 'so that' clause — it holds the reason.

passages.title: The Understudy
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
For two years Neve was the understudy in a play she never performed. Her contract required her to attend every performance in ordinary clothes, to learn every change the director made, and to remain within fifteen minutes of the theatre. In exchange she received a modest wage and a form of readiness that had no outlet.

The condition is stranger than it sounds. An actor who performs is corrected nightly by an audience; she learns which silences hold and which collapse. An understudy is corrected by nobody. Neve rehearsed alone on Monday mornings, delivering a role to empty chairs, and her work grew steadily more precise and steadily less alive, in the way a plant kept from light grows tall and pale at the same time.

On the final Thursday of the run, the lead actor tore a ligament on the stairs, and Neve went on. The notices the next day were respectful rather than warm. One critic wrote that her performance was flawless, which Neve understood, correctly, as a complaint.

She left the profession within the year, though not out of bitterness. She had simply learned what she had been missing, and the lesson was expensive enough that she preferred to spend the rest of it elsewhere.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the main idea?
choices: Practising without an audience can make a performance technically perfect and emotionally dead.
Theatre contracts treat understudies unfairly and should be rewritten.
Neve was never talented enough to hold a leading role.
A single injury can end one actor's career and begin another's.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph argues that an understudy is corrected by nobody, and the review calls her flawless — correct but not moving. That is the passage's argument.

questions.stem: What did Neve's contract require?
choices: That she perform once a month in place of the lead.
That she rehearse with the full cast every Monday.
That she train a second understudy herself.
That she attend every performance and stay within fifteen minutes of the theatre.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph lists the requirements: attend every performance in ordinary clothes, learn every change, and remain within fifteen minutes of the theatre.

questions.stem: Why does Neve treat the word "flawless" as a complaint?
choices: She believes the critic did not actually watch the play.
It praises her accuracy while saying nothing about feeling — which is exactly what her years alone cost her.
The critic used the word about the lead actor as well.
She had made two obvious errors that the critic failed to notice.
questions.explanation: Her work had become more precise and less alive. 'Flawless' names the precision and passes over the life, so the compliment confirms what she had lost.

questions.stem: In "a modest wage," modest means —
choices: paid only after the run ended
shy about being noticed
small, but not insultingly so
earned without a written contract
questions.explanation: The wage is set against a job with heavy demands and no performance, so 'modest' here describes an amount that is small and unremarkable.

lesson.strategy: The passage is an argument dressed as a story: a situation, a comparison that explains why the situation harms her, an event that proves it, and a quiet ending. The comparison in paragraph two — performing actor against understudy — is the engine of the piece, so read it slowly and hold both sides in mind.

signals.phrase: The condition is stranger than it sounds.
signals.means: The writer is about to explain why the obvious reading is too shallow.

signals.phrase: An understudy is corrected by nobody.
signals.means: The key claim, stated bare. Everything else supports it.

signals.phrase: in the way a plant kept from light grows tall and pale at the same time
signals.means: A comparison that carries the whole idea: growth in one direction, loss in another.

signals.phrase: which Neve understood, correctly, as a complaint
signals.means: Irony marker. A word of praise is being read as criticism, and the writer confirms the reading is right.

vocab.inContext: an actor who learns a role in order to replace the main actor if needed
small in amount, without being shockingly low
exact and correct in every detail
lasting anger or resentment about being treated badly

skillTips.main-idea: When a passage builds a comparison, the main idea usually lives in the contrast, not in the plot events.
skillTips.inference: For irony, ask what the praise leaves out. The missing quality is the point.
skillTips.vocabulary: Adjectives about money or size are judged against their context. A demanding job with a small payment tells you what 'modest' means here.
skillTips.detail: Contracts and lists invite invented details. Only choose an option whose words you can find in the text.

passages.title: A Faithful Version
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Halvard Sunde spent thirty-one years translating a single poet, and was praised, in the obituaries, for his fidelity. The word was chosen carefully by people who had not compared the two halves of his work.

He began as a literalist, like a man who distrusts his own taste. The early volumes read like sworn statements: correct, joyless, footnoted where the original had merely been strange. Critics called this rigor, and he accepted the compliment for a decade before admitting that he had produced an exact record of sentences and lost the poems entirely.

The later volumes were another matter. He cut a line that would not survive the crossing. He moved a season. Where the poet had used a proverb no reader here could hear, he substituted one they could, and defended the theft: the poem, not the sentence, was the unit of obligation. His publisher was uneasy. His readers were not; they wept in the right places, which is the only evidence available.

The irony arrived posthumously. A scholar, comparing the two periods, praised the early work as the honest one. Sunde had spent his second life discovering that faithfulness to a text and faithfulness to its effect are different loyalties — and the tribute he finally received belonged to the man he had stopped being.

questions.stem: Which statement best expresses the passage's central point?
choices: Translators should never alter a poet's original wording.
Sunde's publisher and his readers wanted incompatible things from the same books.
Sunde came to believe that being true to a poem's effect is not the same as being true to its words, and he was finally honoured for the approach he had abandoned.
The reputation of a translator depends mostly on the poet he chooses.
questions.explanation: The closing sentences name both halves: two different kinds of faithfulness, and a tribute that belonged to the man he had stopped being.

questions.stem: How did the critics respond to Sunde's early volumes?
choices: They called the exactness of the work rigor and praised it.
They said the footnotes ruined the poems.
They ignored them until the later volumes appeared.
They accused him of inventing lines the poet never wrote.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says critics called this rigor, and he accepted the compliment for a decade.

questions.stem: Why is the scholar's praise described as an irony?
choices: The scholar had not read the poet in the original language.
The obituaries had already said the same thing.
Sunde had asked in his will that the early volumes be withdrawn.
It honours the method Sunde judged a failure and abandoned, not the one he spent his second life defending.
questions.explanation: Sunde had concluded that his early literal work lost the poems. Being praised for exactly that work reverses his own verdict on it.

questions.stem: In "The irony arrived posthumously," posthumously means —
choices: very slowly, over many years
after the person's death
without any public notice
in a foreign country
questions.explanation: The passage opens with his obituaries and ends with a scholar assessing his completed career, so the praise reaches him only after he has died.

lesson.strategy: This is a two-period portrait built for a final reversal: early method, late method, then a judgement that lands on the wrong one. Track the pair of opposed values — exactness against effect — and hold both until the last sentence, where the irony depends on remembering which method Sunde himself rejected.

signals.phrase: The word was chosen carefully by people who had not compared the two halves of his work.
signals.means: An early warning that the praise is unearned or misplaced. It sets up the ending.

signals.phrase: He began as a literalist
signals.means: Opens period one. Expect a contrasting period two.

signals.phrase: The later volumes were another matter.
signals.means: The pivot into period two, with the opposite method.

signals.phrase: which is the only evidence available
signals.means: A dry aside defending his choice: readers' tears are the sole test of whether a poem worked.

signals.phrase: The irony arrived posthumously.
signals.means: The writer names the reversal outright; the sentences after it explain what was reversed.

vocab.inContext: faithfulness — how closely a translation stays true to the original
someone who translates word for word rather than by sense or effect
put one thing in place of another, here a local proverb in place of a foreign one
after the person has died

skillTips.main-idea: With a two-period structure, refuse any answer that names only one period. The main idea must contain the contrast and its outcome.
skillTips.inference: Irony questions are checked against the character's own judgement. Sunde called his early work a failure; that is the fact the praise collides with.
skillTips.vocabulary: Formal words are often unlocked by frame details: obituaries at the start and a scholar reviewing a finished career at the end fix 'posthumously' as after death.
skillTips.detail: Attribute each opinion to its owner — critics, publisher, readers, scholar. The passage gives each a different verdict.

passages.title: Why Ice Floats
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Drop a stone in water and it sinks. Drop a cube of ice in water and it floats. This is strange. Most things get smaller and heavier when they cool. Water does not follow that rule.

When water cools toward freezing, its tiny parts, called molecules, begin to lock together. They form an open pattern with small gaps inside. Because of these gaps, ice takes up more room than the same amount of liquid water. It is less dense, so it rises to the top.

This small habit of water changes whole lakes. In winter, a lake freezes from the surface down. The sheet of ice acts like a lid. It holds the cold above and keeps the water below near four degrees Celsius. Fish, frogs, and plants pass the winter under that lid.

If ice sank, the story would end differently. Each new sheet would drop to the bottom, and the lake would freeze solid from below. Little would survive until spring.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: How fish and frogs find food under a frozen lake.
Why water takes up more room as ice, and what that means for lakes.
How to measure the weight of a stone in water.
Why every liquid gets heavier when it cools.
questions.explanation: The first two paragraphs explain why ice takes up more room and floats; the last two show how the floating layer protects life in a lake.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what does the sheet of ice on a lake do?
choices: It sinks slowly to the bottom over the winter.
It pulls cold water up to the surface.
It acts like a lid and keeps the water below near four degrees Celsius.
It breaks apart each time new snow falls on it.
questions.explanation: The text says the sheet of ice acts like a lid, holds the cold above, and keeps the water below near four degrees Celsius.

questions.stem: What does the passage suggest about most other substances?
choices: In solid form they would sink in their own liquid.
They stay exactly the same size when they cool.
They float even more easily than ice does.
They can only freeze inside a lake.
questions.explanation: The text says most things get smaller and heavier when they cool and that water does not follow that rule. A smaller, heavier solid would sink.

questions.stem: In this passage, 'dense' describes something that is:
choices: very cold to touch
full of small holes
easy to break apart
heavy for the space it fills
questions.explanation: Ice is called less dense because the same amount of water takes up more room as ice. Dense means heavy for the space something fills.

lesson.strategy: This passage sets up a puzzle, explains it, then shows why the puzzle matters. Read the first paragraph as the question, the second as the answer, and the last two as the result in the real world. Do not stop at the science; the point arrives in the lake.

signals.phrase: This is strange.
signals.means: The writer is marking a surprise. An explanation is coming next.

signals.phrase: Because of these gaps
signals.means: A cause. The gaps are the reason for what follows.

signals.phrase: so it rises to the top
signals.means: A result. 'So' links the cause just given to its effect.

signals.phrase: If ice sank
signals.means: An imagined case, not a fact. The writer is showing what would happen in a different world.

vocab.inContext: the tiny parts that water is made of
heavy for the amount of space it fills
a cover on top, here the ice covering the lake
a wide, flat layer of ice

skillTips.main-idea: When a text asks a question early and answers it, the main idea is the answer plus its effect, not the opening picture.
skillTips.inference: Sentences like 'Water does not follow that rule' tell you about everything else by contrast. Ask what the rule means for the other cases.
skillTips.vocabulary: 'Dense' is explained by the sentence before it: more room for the same amount. Use the neighbouring sentence, not a dictionary.
skillTips.detail: Numbers and comparisons ('four degrees Celsius') are easy to check. Go back and find the exact line before choosing.

passages.title: Counting Toward Thunder
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A flash of lightning and the crash of thunder begin at the same moment. You see the flash first because light travels much faster than sound. Light crosses the sky almost at once. Sound needs about three seconds to travel one kilometre.

So you can turn the delay into a measurement. Count the seconds between the flash and the first rumble, then divide by three. The answer is the rough distance to the strike in kilometres. Nine seconds means the lightning was about three kilometres away.

Thunder itself is made of air. Lightning heats the narrow channel it passes through to a temperature far hotter than the surface of the sun. The air in that channel expands in an instant and pushes hard on the air around it. That push spreads outward as a wave, and your ear hears a crash.

Near strikes sound sharp and short. Distant ones sound like a long roll, because the sound reaches you from different parts of the same long channel at slightly different times.

questions.stem: What is the main point of the passage?
choices: Thunder is more dangerous than lightning.
Counting seconds is the only safe thing to do in a storm.
The gap between the flash and the crash has a simple cause, and it can be used to measure distance.
Sound and light leave a lightning strike at different moments.
questions.explanation: The passage explains why the sound arrives late, turns that delay into a distance, and then explains what makes the sound.

questions.stem: How far does sound travel in about three seconds, according to the passage?
choices: One kilometre
Three kilometres
Nine kilometres
As far as light does
questions.explanation: The first paragraph states that sound needs about three seconds to travel one kilometre.

questions.stem: A person counts fifteen seconds between the flash and the crash. What does the passage suggest?
choices: The lightning was weaker than usual.
The sound and the light started at different times.
The strike was about fifteen kilometres away.
The strike was about five kilometres away.
questions.explanation: The rule given is to divide the seconds by three, so fifteen seconds means roughly five kilometres.

questions.stem: In this passage, 'channel' means:
choices: the narrow path the lightning follows through the air
a wide, open field below the cloud
a deep cut in the ground
a way of sending a radio signal
questions.explanation: The text says lightning heats 'the narrow channel it passes through', so the channel is the thin path of the strike.

lesson.strategy: The passage moves from an observation, to a rule you can use, to the cause behind it. Hold on to the numbers in the first two paragraphs, because one question will ask you to use them. The last paragraph explains a difference in sound, not a difference in danger.

signals.phrase: You see the flash first because
signals.means: A cause is about to be given for something you already noticed.

signals.phrase: So you can turn the delay into a measurement.
signals.means: The writer shifts from fact to practical use. A method follows.

signals.phrase: That push spreads outward as a wave
signals.means: One step in a chain: heat, then push, then wave, then sound.

signals.phrase: because the sound reaches you from different parts of the same long channel
signals.means: The reason for the long rolling sound of far-off thunder.

vocab.inContext: the waiting time between the flash and the sound
a low, rolling sound
the narrow path the lightning cuts through the air
gets bigger fast, pushing outward

skillTips.main-idea: If a text gives a method, the main idea usually includes both the method and the reason it works.
skillTips.inference: Some inference questions ask you to apply a rule to a new number. Find the rule, then do the small calculation.
skillTips.vocabulary: Adjectives next to a word are clues. 'Narrow channel it passes through' tells you channel is a path.
skillTips.detail: Watch for two similar numbers (three seconds, three kilometres). Reread which one goes with which unit.

passages.title: Two Lives, One Body
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
The grey-green crust on an old stone wall looks like a single plant. It is not a plant at all, and it is not a single organism. A lichen is a partnership: a fungus that builds the body, and an alga or a bacterium that makes food inside it.

The division of labour is clear. The fungus cannot make its own food, but it can grip bare rock, hold water, and shield its partner from strong light. The alga has no roots and no shelter, but it can turn sunlight into sugar. Together they live where neither could live alone, on gravestones, on bark, on stone in the high mountains.

The cost of the arrangement is speed. Many lichens grow less than a millimetre a year, and some patches on Arctic rock are centuries old. The cost is also exposure. A lichen has no waxy skin and no way to shut itself off from the air, so it absorbs whatever the air carries, clean or dirty. Where pollution is heavy, lichens thin out and vanish before most other life shows harm. Scientists read that absence as a warning.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the main idea?
choices: Lichens are unusual plants that grow on stone walls and gravestones.
A lichen is two organisms living as one, and that deal brings both power and cost.
Fungi are more important to a lichen than algae are.
Air pollution is the greatest danger facing mountain plants.
questions.explanation: The passage defines the partnership, shows what each partner gives, then names its two costs: slow growth and exposure to the air.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what does the fungus contribute to the partnership?
choices: It turns sunlight into sugar.
It grows roots deep into the rock.
It grips the rock, holds water, and shields its partner from strong light.
It filters dirty air before the alga can absorb it.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph lists exactly these three jobs for the fungus; making sugar from sunlight is the alga's job.

questions.stem: Lichens have disappeared from the trees of a city park. What can you reasonably infer?
choices: The air in that area is probably polluted.
The trees in the park are too young to carry lichens.
The lichens have moved to the stone walls nearby.
The park receives too much sunlight for any lichen.
questions.explanation: The text says lichens absorb whatever the air carries and vanish first where pollution is heavy, and that scientists read their absence as a warning.

questions.stem: In this passage, 'shield' means:
choices: measure carefully
feed steadily
carry from place to place
protect from something harmful
questions.explanation: The fungus shields its partner from strong light, that is, it protects the alga from light that would harm it.

lesson.strategy: This passage corrects a wrong first impression, then explains a trade. Paragraph two is the benefit side, paragraph three is the cost side. Track who does what: mixing up the fungus and the alga is the easiest mistake here.

signals.phrase: It is not a plant at all
signals.means: The writer is correcting what you assumed in the first sentence.

signals.phrase: The division of labour is clear.
signals.means: A list is coming: which partner does which job.

signals.phrase: Together they live where neither could live alone
signals.means: The core claim, that the pair can do what each alone cannot.

signals.phrase: The cost of the arrangement is speed.
signals.means: A turn from benefits to costs. A second cost will follow.

vocab.inContext: two different living things working together as one body
protect from harm, here from light that is too strong
being open to whatever is in the air, with no protection
takes in from around it, without choosing

skillTips.main-idea: When a text names both a benefit and a cost, the main idea has to hold both. A choice that keeps only one half is too narrow.
skillTips.inference: The last line, 'Scientists read that absence as a warning', invites you to apply the idea to a new place. Use the stated cause.
skillTips.vocabulary: Read what the word acts on: 'shield its partner from strong light' shows shield is about protection.
skillTips.detail: For two-partner texts, make a quick mental table: fungus does X, alga does Y. Then match the option to the right column.

passages.title: What Sleep Does With The Day
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Sleep looks like a pause, but the brain does not stop. In the hours after learning, it replays the day.

Researchers who record brain activity in sleeping animals see the same patterns of firing that appeared during the day's tasks, run again in compressed bursts. The idea, supported by many experiments, is that a new memory first sits in a fast, fragile store and is slowly copied into a slower, more durable one. Sleep is when much of that copying happens.

Human studies point the same way. People who learn a list of words and then sleep remember more of it than people who learn the same list and stay awake for the same number of hours. The advantage is not simply time away from the material; a nap of an hour or two can produce it, while the same hours spent awake and busy usually do not.

This is why an all-night session before an exam is a poor trade. Extra hours of reading buy material that the brain is given no time to file. That filing is called consolidation, and it is not a luxury added after learning. It is the second half of learning itself.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly arguing?
choices: Animal brains and human brains work in exactly the same way.
Students should read less and rest more in general.
Word lists are the best way to test memory.
Sleep is an active part of learning, not simply a rest afterwards.
questions.explanation: Every paragraph builds the claim that memory is copied and fixed during sleep, ending with 'It is the second half of learning itself.'

questions.stem: What do researchers see in the brains of sleeping animals?
choices: Firing patterns from the day's tasks running again in compressed bursts.
Almost no activity until the animal wakes.
New patterns that never appeared while the animal was awake.
Activity only in animals that learned nothing that day.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph states this directly: the same patterns of firing from the day's tasks, run again in compressed bursts.

questions.stem: Two students study the same material. Alba studies for two hours and sleeps eight. Ben studies for four hours and sleeps four. What does the passage suggest?
choices: Ben will remember more, because he read the material twice as long.
Alba may remember more, because her brain gets more time to file what she read.
Neither will remember anything without a nap during the day.
Both will remember the same amount, since they were awake for equal time.
questions.explanation: The passage says extra reading buys material the brain has no time to file, and that sleepers recall more than those who stay awake.

questions.stem: In this passage, 'fragile' describes a memory store that is:
choices: extremely large
shared between two people
easily lost or damaged
very slow to fill
questions.explanation: The fragile store is contrasted with a 'more durable' one, so fragile means easily lost, not lasting.

lesson.strategy: This is an argument built from two kinds of evidence: animal recordings first, then human experiments. The last paragraph turns the evidence into advice. Read for the contrast pair fast and fragile against slow and durable, because the whole argument sits on it.

signals.phrase: but the brain does not stop
signals.means: A contrast with the everyday view of sleep. The real claim starts here.

signals.phrase: The idea, supported by many experiments, is that
signals.means: The writer is careful: this is a theory with evidence, not a proven fact.

signals.phrase: Human studies point the same way.
signals.means: A second, independent line of evidence agreeing with the first.

signals.phrase: This is why an all-night session before an exam is a poor trade.
signals.means: The turn from evidence to practical conclusion.

vocab.inContext: squeezed into a shorter time than the original
easily lost, not yet firmly held
lasting, able to survive over time
the brain's work of filing a new memory into lasting storage

skillTips.main-idea: When each paragraph adds evidence for one claim, the last sentence is often the cleanest statement of the main idea.
skillTips.inference: Apply the argument to the case in the question. Ask which person the text's rule would favour, and why.
skillTips.vocabulary: Contrast pairs teach meaning. 'Fragile' sits opposite 'more durable', so it must mean the reverse.
skillTips.detail: Careful phrases like 'supported by many experiments' matter. A choice that states the theory as certain is a different claim.

passages.title: The Diary Inside A Tree
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Cut across the trunk of an old oak and you meet a set of rings. In climates with a real winter, the tree adds one ring a year: pale, quick wood in spring, dark, tight wood late in the season. Count the rings and you have the age of the tree. Measure their width and you have something better, a record of the years themselves.

A wet, mild year leaves a wide ring. A drought leaves a narrow one. Because every tree in a region meets the same weather, the trees of that region share one pattern of wide and narrow bands, like a barcode.

That shared pattern lets researchers reach back further than any living tree. A beam cut from an old farmhouse carries rings too, and if the outer rings of the beam match the inner rings of a living trunk, the two records can be joined. Chain enough overlaps together and the sequence runs back thousands of years, with every ring tied to an exact calendar year.

Archaeologists use those sequences to date buildings and ships. Climate scientists use them to test what the weather did long before anyone wrote it down.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: How to tell an oak tree from other kinds of tree.
Why old farmhouses were built from oak beams.
How tree rings record past years and can be joined into a long dated record.
Why trees grow faster in warm regions than in cold ones.
questions.explanation: The passage moves from one tree's rings, to the shared regional pattern, to chained overlaps that reach back thousands of years.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what does a narrow ring show?
choices: That the tree was cut down that year.
That the year was dry.
That the tree was very young.
That two rings grew in one season.
questions.explanation: The text pairs a wet, mild year with a wide ring and a drought with a narrow one.

questions.stem: What must be true before a wooden beam can be given an exact calendar date?
choices: The tree it came from must still be alive somewhere.
The beam must come from the same farmhouse as another dated beam.
The beam must be older than any living tree in the region.
Its ring pattern must overlap with a pattern that is already dated.
questions.explanation: Dating works by matching the beam's rings to an existing sequence; without an overlap, the beam cannot be tied to calendar years.

questions.stem: In this passage, 'beam' means:
choices: a long piece of timber used to build with
a line of bright light
a wide smile
a ring of new spring wood
questions.explanation: The beam is 'cut from an old farmhouse' and 'carries rings', so it is a piece of building timber.

lesson.strategy: The passage widens step by step: one tree, then one region, then thousands of years. Each paragraph depends on the one before it, so if a step is unclear, go back rather than forward. The final paragraph only names who uses the method.

signals.phrase: In climates with a real winter
signals.means: A limit on the claim. The one-ring-a-year rule does not hold everywhere.

signals.phrase: Because every tree in a region meets the same weather
signals.means: The cause that makes the shared pattern possible.

signals.phrase: like a barcode
signals.means: A comparison. The pattern is unique and can be matched, like a code.

signals.phrase: That shared pattern lets researchers reach back further than any living tree.
signals.means: The key move of the passage: from living wood to old wood.

vocab.inContext: a long stretch of time with too little rain
a long piece of cut timber inside a building
sections where two ring records cover the same years
a run of years placed in order, one after another

skillTips.main-idea: In a step-by-step explainer, the main idea is the whole chain, not the first step. Prefer the choice that covers the last step too.
skillTips.inference: Ask what a method needs in order to work. Here, matching requires an overlap, even though the text never says 'must'.
skillTips.vocabulary: A word with several everyday meanings, like 'beam', is fixed by its verbs: it is cut, and it carries rings.
skillTips.detail: Pairs (wide and wet, narrow and dry) are common detail traps. Reread the pairing before you answer.

passages.title: Why Antibiotics Lose Power
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
An antibiotic does not teach bacteria to resist it. The resistance is already present in a handful of cells, produced by ordinary copying errors long before the drug arrives. What the drug does is edit the population: it kills the cells that cannot survive it and leaves the rare ones that can. Those survivors then divide in an emptied field, with their competition gone, and within days the resistant type is no longer rare.

Two features of bacteria make this loop unusually fast. The first is speed of reproduction; a population can double in twenty minutes, so a number of generations that a mammal would need centuries to produce can pass in a single weekend.
