signals.phrase: One end loves water. The other end loves oil.
signals.means: The key fact. Two opposite ends on one piece is the whole trick.

signals.phrase: It simply gives the dirt a handle that water can hold.
signals.means: The main idea restated as a picture. A good sentence to remember.

vocab.inContext: thick oil or fat, the kind that sticks to hands and pans
wash with clean water so the loose stuff runs off
cover something completely on all sides
the hole and pipe that carries used water away

skillTips.main-idea: When a passage names a problem and then a solution, the main idea is the solution, not the problem.
skillTips.inference: An inference is one small step past the words. The text says water and oil pull apart; you conclude that is why grease stays without soap.
skillTips.vocabulary: Look at what happens around the word. "Rinse" comes right before the grease goes down the drain, so it must involve water carrying something off.
skillTips.detail: Detail answers sit in one sentence. Find that sentence and match it word for word before you choose.

passages.title: Why We Shiver
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Your body works best at one temperature, near 37 degrees Celsius. It holds that number all day, in summer and in winter. When the air turns cold, your body starts to lose heat to the air around it. Something has to replace that heat.

So the body makes its own. Deep in the brain sits a small control center that watches your temperature the way a thermostat watches a room. When the number begins to drop, it sends a signal to your muscles: move. The muscles tighten and release, tighten and release, many times a second. That is a shiver.

Moving muscles always give off heat. A runner gets hot for the same reason. Shivering uses that fact on purpose. The shaking does no work you can see, and you did not choose it, but it warms you from the inside. This is also why shivering is tiring. The heat is not free. Your body is burning fuel to buy it back.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: Why cold weather makes people want to move indoors.
How shivering is the body making heat to hold its temperature.
Why runners get hot when they exercise.
How the brain controls every muscle in the body.
questions.explanation: Each paragraph builds the same point: the body must stay near 37 degrees, cold air steals heat, so the muscles shake to make heat back. The runner is only an example.

questions.stem: In this passage, a "thermostat" is best understood as something that
choices: makes a room colder
measures how much fuel is left
burns fuel to make heat
watches a temperature and acts when it changes
questions.explanation: The text says the control center "watches your temperature the way a thermostat watches a room," and then it acts by signalling the muscles. Watching and acting is the point of the comparison.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what does the control center in the brain do when your temperature starts to drop?
choices: It signals the muscles to move.
It slows the blood down.
It raises the temperature of the air.
It tells you to put on a coat.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph states it directly: it sends a signal to your muscles: move. The other choices are never mentioned.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that shivering makes you tired because
choices: the shaking keeps you from sleeping
cold air is harder to breathe
your body spends fuel to make the heat
your muscles are damaged by the cold
questions.explanation: The last two sentences say the heat is not free and the body is burning fuel to buy it back. Spending fuel is what makes it tiring. Sleep, breathing, and damage are not mentioned.

lesson.strategy: This passage explains a chain: cold air, lost heat, a signal, a shiver. Follow the chain in order and ask at each step what causes the next one. The last three sentences add a cost, which is a small surprise worth noticing.

signals.phrase: It holds that number all day
signals.means: Sets up the rule the whole passage depends on: the temperature must stay steady.

signals.phrase: So the body makes its own.
signals.means: "So" marks a result. Heat was lost, so heat must be made.

signals.phrase: That is a shiver.
signals.means: The writer names the thing only after describing it. The definition is here.

signals.phrase: The heat is not free.
signals.means: A turn to the cost. Expect the reason for tiredness right after.

vocab.inContext: how hot or cold something is, as a number
a device that watches temperature and switches heating on or off
a message sent to make something happen
the energy a body or machine burns to do work

skillTips.main-idea: If every paragraph returns to the same idea, that idea is the main one. Here it is holding a steady temperature.
skillTips.inference: The text rarely says "because" for the last step. It says fuel is burned; you connect that to being tired.
skillTips.vocabulary: A comparison often defines a word for you. "The way a thermostat watches a room" tells you what a thermostat does.
skillTips.detail: When a question says "according to the passage," the answer is written down. Do not reason; find it.

passages.title: Why a Week Has Seven Days
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A day is the earth turning once. A year is the earth going around the sun. A month is close to the moon's round of changes. These units come from the sky. You can see them.

A week is different. Nothing in nature takes exactly seven days. So where did the number come from? The answer goes back to ancient Babylon, more than three thousand years ago. Sky watchers there counted the lights that moved against the fixed stars. They found seven: the sun, the moon, and five points we now call planets. Seven moving lights, seven days.

The idea travelled. It reached Greece, then Rome, and Roman names for those lights became names for the days. Some of them are still in our week. Later, other peoples replaced some Roman names with their own gods, which is why the English days sound less Roman than the French or Spanish ones. The count of seven never changed. A week is not a piece of nature. It is a very old habit that we agreed to keep.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: The seven-day week came from an old human count, not from nature.
The Romans invented the week and gave it to the rest of Europe.
The moon takes seven days to change its shape.
Ancient people knew more about the sky than we do today.
questions.explanation: The passage contrasts the day, month, and year, which come from the sky, with the week, which does not. It ends by saying a week is a very old habit we agreed to keep.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what did the sky watchers of Babylon count?
choices: Seven bright stars that never moved.
The days between one full moon and the next.
Seven lights that moved against the fixed stars.
The number of gods in their religion.
questions.explanation: The text says they counted the lights that moved against the fixed stars and found seven: the sun, the moon, and five planets. The fixed stars are the background, not the count.

questions.stem: In this passage, "fixed" stars are stars that
choices: are very bright
stay in the same place relative to each other
were repaired by astronomers
can only be seen in winter
questions.explanation: The moving lights are counted "against the fixed stars," so the fixed stars are the still background that makes the movement visible. Here "fixed" means not moving.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that English day names differ from French ones because
choices: English speakers could not pronounce the Roman names
England adopted the week much later than France did
the English week once had a different number of days
some peoples swapped the Roman gods for gods of their own
questions.explanation: The text says other peoples replaced some Roman names with their own gods, which is why English sounds less Roman. It also says the count of seven never changed anywhere.

lesson.strategy: The first paragraph sets a pattern, and the second breaks it. Read for that break: three units come from the sky, and then one does not. Once you see the question the writer is asking, the rest of the passage is the answer.

signals.phrase: These units come from the sky.
signals.means: The pattern. Hold on to it, because the next line will break it.

signals.phrase: A week is different.
signals.means: The turn. The writer is now on the real subject.

signals.phrase: So where did the number come from?
signals.means: The question the rest of the passage answers. Everything after is the answer.

signals.phrase: The count of seven never changed.
signals.means: Names changed, the number did not. A useful contrast to keep straight.

vocab.inContext: from a time very long ago
staying in the same place, not moving
here, spread from place to place as an idea
put something new in the place of something old

skillTips.main-idea: A passage that asks a direct question usually states its main idea in the answer, near the end.
skillTips.inference: Link two sentences the writer left apart: other peoples used their own gods, and English sounds less Roman.
skillTips.vocabulary: Contrast gives meaning. "Moved" against "fixed" tells you fixed means not moving.
skillTips.detail: Watch small words in the choices. "Stars that never moved" and "lights that moved" are opposites here.

passages.title: The Girl Who Found the Sea Dragon
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Mary Anning was born in 1799 in Lyme Regis, a small town on the south coast of England. The cliffs there are full of fossils, the stone shapes of animals that died long ago. Her family was poor. They collected fossils from the beach and sold them to visitors.

When Mary was about twelve, her brother found a strange skull in the cliff. Mary kept digging. Over months she uncovered a whole skeleton, long and narrow, with wide eyes and rows of teeth. People called it a sea dragon. Today we call it an ichthyosaur. It was a reptile that swam in an ocean that once covered England.

Mary went on digging for the rest of her life. She found other creatures no one had seen before, and scientists came to her for help. But she could not join the Geological Society of London, because it did not accept women. Men wrote the papers about her finds, and often left her name out. The bones are still in museums today. So is the argument about who gets the credit.

questions.stem: In this passage, "fossils" are
choices: stones that look like coins
shells that wash up after a storm
tools used to dig into a cliff
the stone shapes of animals that died long ago
questions.explanation: The passage defines the word in the same sentence: fossils are "the stone shapes of animals that died long ago."

questions.stem: According to the passage, why could Mary Anning not join the Geological Society of London?
choices: She lived too far from the city.
It did not accept women.
Her family could not pay the fee.
She had never been to school.
questions.explanation: The text gives one reason: it did not accept women. Her family's poverty is mentioned earlier, but not as the reason for this.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the main idea?
choices: Lyme Regis is a good place to look for fossils.
Sea dragons once swam in an ocean over England.
Mary Anning made important discoveries but was denied the credit for them.
Poor families in England often worked on the beach.
questions.explanation: The passage follows her finds and ends on the credit she was denied. The last two sentences make that the point. The other choices are details inside the story.

questions.stem: The last sentence, "So is the argument about who gets the credit," suggests that
choices: people still discuss whether Mary Anning was treated fairly
museums are unsure which bones she actually found
scientists no longer believe her discoveries were real
her family later sold the skeleton to another country
questions.explanation: "So is" carries over the word "still" from the sentence before: the bones are still in museums, and the argument is still going on. The passage never questions that the finds were hers or real.

lesson.strategy: This is a life story told in order, but the point is not the order. Watch what the writer chooses to end on. The last two sentences turn a story about bones into a story about credit.

signals.phrase: Her family was poor.
signals.means: Explains why a child was on the beach selling fossils. Background, not the point.

signals.phrase: Mary kept digging.
signals.means: Her brother found the skull; she did the long work. The writer is being careful here.

signals.phrase: But she could not join
signals.means: "But" turns the passage. Success is about to meet a wall.

signals.phrase: So is the argument about who gets the credit.
signals.means: The real ending. "So is" means this also is still true today.

vocab.inContext: stone shapes left behind by animals that died long ago
the full set of bones of one animal
a cold-blooded animal with scales, like a lizard or crocodile
public recognition for having done something

skillTips.main-idea: In a life story, the main idea is usually what the writer spends the ending on, not the earliest event.
skillTips.inference: Short sentences that begin with "So is" or "So was" point back. Find what they point to.
skillTips.vocabulary: Writers often define a hard word right where they use it, inside a comma pair.
skillTips.detail: If two facts could both explain something, pick the one the passage links directly to the question.

passages.title: Why a List Helps
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Try to hold a phone number, a shopping list, and a friend's question in your head at the same time. Something slips. This is normal. The part of the mind that holds what you are using right now is small. It can keep only a few things at once, and each new thing pushes an old one out.

A list moves the load out of your head and onto the paper. The paper does not forget. Now the small space in your mind is free for the work itself, instead of the effort of remembering what the work is.

This is why a list often helps even when you never read it again. Writing the tasks down ends the quiet job of holding them. It also turns a vague worry into a fixed number of items, and a fixed number feels smaller than a cloud. Good lists are short and plain. A list of thirty items becomes a new thing to worry about, which is the problem it was supposed to solve.

questions.stem: What is the main point of the passage?
choices: Most people forget their shopping lists.
Paper is a more reliable material than memory.
A list helps by taking the job of remembering out of a small mental space.
Writing by hand is better than typing on a phone.
questions.explanation: The passage explains that the mind holds only a few things at once, and a list moves that load onto paper so the mind is free. That is the argument from start to end.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that a list of thirty items is a problem because
choices: long lists take too much time to write
people usually lose lists that are long
thirty items cannot fit on one page
it becomes another load to worry about
questions.explanation: The last sentence says a list of thirty items becomes a new thing to worry about, which is the problem it was supposed to solve. Time, losing it, and page size are not mentioned.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what happens when a new thing enters the small space in your mind?
choices: It pushes an old thing out.
It is stored until the end of the day.
It makes the space grow a little.
It is copied onto paper automatically.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph states it: it can keep only a few things at once, and each new thing pushes an old one out.

questions.stem: In this passage, "vague" means
choices: written down carefully
not clear, without a definite shape
very urgent
shared with other people
questions.explanation: "A vague worry" is contrasted with "a fixed number of items" and compared to a cloud. So vague means unclear and without a definite shape.

lesson.strategy: The passage argues a case. Find the claim, then find the reason under it. The claim is that lists help; the reason is that your working memory is small. The final paragraph adds a limit, so do not stop reading early.

signals.phrase: Something slips.
signals.means: The demonstration. The writer makes you feel the problem before naming it.

signals.phrase: The paper does not forget.
signals.means: The core of the argument, in four words.

signals.phrase: even when you never read it again
signals.means: A surprising claim. The reason for it comes in the next sentence.

signals.phrase: Good lists are short and plain.
signals.means: A limit on the advice. Expect the cost of ignoring it right after.

vocab.inContext: an amount of work or weight that something has to carry
unclear, without a definite shape or edge
settled, not changing
simple and easy to understand

skillTips.main-idea: In an argument, the main idea is the claim plus its reason, not just the advice at the end.
skillTips.inference: When a passage says something "becomes the problem it was meant to solve," it is telling you the cost. Name that cost.
skillTips.vocabulary: Use the contrast. "Vague" sits opposite "a fixed number," so it must mean unfixed and unclear.
skillTips.detail: Detail questions often quote the passage almost exactly. Match the wording.

passages.title: How Your Phone Knows Where You Are
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Open a map on your phone and a blue dot appears. The phone did not ask anyone where you are. It worked it out, and it did so by listening to clocks in space.

High above the earth, satellites circle in fixed paths. Each one carries a very accurate clock and sends out a steady signal. The signal says two things: which satellite is speaking, and the exact time the message left. The signal travels at the speed of light, which is fast but not instant. Your phone reads the time in the message, compares it with the time now, and turns that tiny gap into a distance.

One distance is not enough. Knowing you are 20,000 kilometres from one satellite places you somewhere on a huge sphere. A second satellite narrows it. With four, the phone can fix your position and correct its own cheap clock at the same time. This is also why the blue dot struggles indoors. The signals are faint, and thick walls are enough to lose them.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what two things does a satellite's signal say?
choices: The weather and the time.
Which satellite is speaking, and the exact time the message left.
Your name and your distance from the satellite.
The height of the satellite and its speed.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph lists them directly: which satellite is speaking, and the exact time the message left.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly explaining?
choices: Why maps on phones are sometimes wrong.
How satellites are launched into space.
How a phone works out its position from satellite signals.
Why the speed of light is important in science.
questions.explanation: Every paragraph builds the same explanation: signals carry a send time, the phone turns the gap into a distance, and several distances fix a position.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that if the speed of light were instant, this method would
choices: no longer work, because there would be no time gap to measure
work much faster than it does now
need more satellites than four
still work, but only outdoors
questions.explanation: The phone turns the tiny gap between the send time and now into a distance. The text points out that light is "fast but not instant." With no gap, there would be nothing to measure.

questions.stem: In this passage, "faint" means
choices: very loud and clear
sent from far away
arriving too late to use
weak and hard to pick up
questions.explanation: The word explains why the dot struggles indoors, alongside thick walls that lose the signals. A weak signal is the reason. Distance alone is not the point, since the satellites are always far away.

lesson.strategy: This explains a machine, so read it as steps. Ask what the phone knows after each paragraph: first that a signal carries a time, then that a time gap is a distance, then that several distances give a point. The last three sentences explain a failure, which is often where the real understanding is tested.

signals.phrase: it did so by listening to clocks in space
signals.means: The whole idea in one line. The rest of the passage unpacks it.

signals.phrase: fast but not instant
signals.means: A small phrase carrying the key fact. Without a delay there is nothing to measure.

signals.phrase: One distance is not enough.
signals.means: A turn. The writer is about to explain why several satellites are needed.

signals.phrase: This is also why
signals.means: The explanation is being used to account for something you have noticed yourself.

vocab.inContext: a machine that circles the earth in a fixed path
a message sent out as a wave
happening with no time passing at all
weak, hard to hear or detect

skillTips.main-idea: For a how-it-works passage, the main idea is the method, not any single part of the machine.
skillTips.inference: Take a stated fact and remove it. If light were instant, the gap the phone measures would vanish. That is the inference.
skillTips.vocabulary: Read the sentence that follows. Thick walls losing signals tells you faint means weak.
skillTips.detail: When a passage says "two things," the answer is a pair. Check that both halves of your choice appear in the text.

passages.title: Why Ants Walk in a Line
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Drop a crumb on the ground and wait. Before long a single ant arrives, then another, and soon a thin dark line runs from the crumb to a crack in the wall. No ant is leading. There is no plan.

The first ant was wandering. When it found the crumb it turned for home, and as it walked it pressed a faint smell onto the ground behind it. Ants can follow that smell. The next ant crosses the trail, turns onto it, finds the food, and walks home leaving its own smell on top. The trail gets stronger each time it is used.

That is the whole system. A short trail is walked more often than a long one in the same time, so short routes get stronger and win. And when the crumb is gone, the ants stop adding smell. The old trail dries into the air and disappears. Nobody gives the order to stop. The line ends because nothing is left to feed it.

questions.stem: In this passage, a "trail" is
choices: a narrow path of smell left on the ground
a line of ants standing still
a crack in the wall where ants live
the crumb the ants are carrying
questions.explanation: The passage says the ant "pressed a faint smell onto the ground behind it" and calls that the trail, which later ants follow and strengthen.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that short routes win because
choices: ants can smell better over short distances
the first ant always chooses the shortest way
a short trail is walked more often, so its smell grows stronger
long trails are washed away by rain
questions.explanation: The text says a short trail is walked more often than a long one in the same time, so short routes get stronger and win. No ant chooses; the smell simply builds up faster.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Ants prefer sweet food to other kinds.
The ant line is organised by smell alone, with no leader and no plan.
Ants live in cracks in walls and come out to hunt.
One ant can carry a crumb much larger than itself.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says there is no leader and no plan; the rest explains how smell alone produces the line, and the last sentence returns to it.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what happens after the crumb is gone?
choices: The ants find a new crumb nearby.
The ants carry the trail back to the nest.
A leader ant calls the others home.
The ants stop adding smell and the trail disappears.
questions.explanation: The text says the ants stop adding smell, the old trail dries into the air and disappears, and nobody gives the order to stop.

lesson.strategy: The writer tells you the puzzle in the first paragraph: a line forms with no leader. Read the rest as the solution, one small rule at a time. Each rule is about one ant, never about the group.

signals.phrase: No ant is leading. There is no plan.
signals.means: The puzzle. Hold this in mind; the passage exists to explain it.

signals.phrase: leaving its own smell on top
signals.means: The loop. Using the trail makes the trail stronger.

signals.phrase: That is the whole system.
signals.means: The writer is telling you nothing more is needed. Simple rules, big result.

signals.phrase: because nothing is left to feed it
signals.means: The ending has the same shape as the beginning: no decision, just a cause.

vocab.inContext: moving around with no fixed direction
weak, only just strong enough to notice
a line left behind that others can follow
the way taken from one place to another

skillTips.main-idea: When a passage opens with a puzzle, the main idea is the answer to that puzzle, stated plainly somewhere later.
skillTips.inference: Follow the loop. More walking means more smell, and more smell means more walking. Short trails simply loop faster.
skillTips.vocabulary: The definition may come before the word. The smell is described first and named "trail" after.
skillTips.detail: Beware of choices that add a leader or a decision. This passage repeats that there is neither.

passages.title: Why the Big Box Costs Less
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Two boxes of the same rice sit on the shelf. The small one holds one kilogram and costs three dollars. The large one holds five kilograms and costs twelve dollars. The large box has a bigger number on the price tag, yet it is the cheaper rice. One kilogram costs three dollars in the small box and two dollars and forty cents in the large one.

The reason is that some costs do not grow with size. The box itself, the printing, the label, the space on the truck, the moment a worker spends handling it: these change very little between one kilogram and five. Spread the same fixed cost over more rice and the cost of each kilogram falls.

This is why shops print a price per kilogram in small letters under the tag. It is the only number that lets you compare. But a lower unit price is a saving only if you use it all. Buy five kilograms, eat one, and throw four away, and you paid twelve dollars for one kilogram. That is the most expensive rice in the shop.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what does one kilogram cost in the large box?
choices: Two dollars and forty cents.
Three dollars.
Twelve dollars.
Five dollars.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph gives both numbers: three dollars per kilogram in the small box and two dollars and forty cents in the large one.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that a shopper who buys the large box and wastes most of it
choices: has still saved money overall
should have bought two small boxes instead
will be refunded the difference
has actually paid the highest price of all
questions.explanation: The last two sentences say that buying five kilograms and using one means paying twelve dollars for one kilogram, which the writer calls the most expensive rice in the shop.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Rice is cheaper than most other foods.
Shops hide the real price of their products.
Large boxes cost less per unit because fixed costs are shared, but only if you use it all.
You should always buy the largest box available.
questions.explanation: The passage explains why the unit price falls (fixed costs spread over more product) and then adds the condition in the last paragraph. Both halves are needed.

questions.stem: In this passage, a "fixed cost" is a cost that
choices: is set by the government
stays about the same no matter how much is in the box
is the largest cost a shop pays
rises as the box gets bigger
questions.explanation: The second paragraph lists box, printing, label, truck space, and handling as costs that "change very little between one kilogram and five." That is what makes them fixed.

lesson.strategy: This passage uses real numbers, so slow down and check them. Work out the per-kilogram price yourself before reading on. Then watch for the turn in the last paragraph, where the writer takes half of the advice back.

signals.phrase: yet it is the cheaper rice
signals.means: "Yet" signals a surprise. A bigger price tag can still be a lower price.

signals.phrase: some costs do not grow with size
signals.means: The reason, stated once and plainly. Everything in the list is an example of it.

signals.phrase: It is the only number that lets you compare.
signals.means: Practical advice built on the explanation above.

signals.phrase: only if you use it all
signals.means: The condition. The rule just given has a limit, and the example follows.

vocab.inContext: the cost of one standard amount, such as one kilogram
here, staying the same no matter how much is being sold
divided across several things
look at two things side by side to see which is better

skillTips.main-idea: When a passage gives a rule and then a condition, the main idea includes both. An answer with only the rule is incomplete.
skillTips.inference: Follow the writer's own example to its end. One kilogram used out of five bought means the full price paid for that one.
skillTips.vocabulary: A list of examples can define a term. Box, label, and truck space all share one feature: they do not change with size.
skillTips.detail: With numbers, check the unit. The question asks per kilogram, not per box.

passages.title: Where the Tap Begins
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Turn a tap in a city and the water arrives in a second. The journey behind it started weeks earlier, and far away.

Rain does not fall on a city and stay there. It falls on hills, roofs, fields, and forests, and gravity pulls it downhill into small streams. Those streams join into larger ones. The whole area of land that drains into a single river is called a watershed, and it can be hundreds of times larger than the city itself.

Somewhere along that river stands a wall of concrete or earth, built across the valley. Behind it the water backs up into a long lake. This is a reservoir: not a natural lake, but a store. Its job is patience. Rain is uneven, and some months bring floods while others bring nothing. A reservoir holds the wet months so the dry ones can be spent.

Everything that follows in a water system rests on this first step. A city can clean water, move it, and price it. It cannot make it.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: Why rain falls unevenly through the year.
How a city's water is collected from a watershed and stored in a reservoir.
How walls of concrete are built across river valleys.
Why water arrives at a tap so quickly.
questions.explanation: The passage follows one path: rain drains off a wide area into a river, and a dam holds that river in a reservoir. The uneven rain and the concrete wall are parts of that story, not the subject of it.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what is a watershed?
choices: The whole area of land that drains into a single river.
The wall that holds water back across a valley.
A building where a city stores water it has cleaned.
A month in which heavy rain falls.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph defines it in one sentence: the whole area of land that drains into a single river. The wall is the dam, described later.

questions.stem: In this passage, a "reservoir" is best understood as
choices: a natural lake high in the hills
a pipe that carries rain off a roof
a store of water held back so it can be used later
a machine that cleans water taken from a river
questions.explanation: The text says plainly that it is "not a natural lake, but a store," and that it holds the wet months so the dry ones can be spent.

questions.stem: The passage says a reservoir's "job is patience." This suggests that
choices: a reservoir takes many years to build
the useful thing a reservoir does is hold water from wet months for dry ones
water tastes better after it has been stored for a while
rivers move too slowly to serve a large city
questions.explanation: Patience here means waiting. The sentences on either side explain the waiting: rain is uneven, so the store carries water from the months that have it to the months that do not.

lesson.strategy: Follow the water backwards. The passage moves from your tap out to the streams, then to the reservoir behind the dam, one stage per paragraph. Hold that order. The last two sentences state the point of the whole chain: a city can move water, not make it.

signals.phrase: The journey behind it started weeks earlier
signals.means: Signals that the passage runs backwards in time, from the tap toward the source.

signals.phrase: is called a watershed
signals.means: A definition is arriving. The words just before it carry the meaning.

signals.phrase: Its job is patience.
signals.means: A figure of speech holding the reservoir's real purpose: waiting out wet and dry months.

signals.phrase: It cannot make it.
signals.means: The closing limit. Every later stage depends on this one fixed supply.

vocab.inContext: the pull that makes water run downhill on its own
all the land whose rain drains into one river
a large store of water held behind a dam for later use

skillTips.main-idea: Three stages, one subject: where a city's water comes from. Choose the answer that covers collecting and storing, not one that names only the rain or only the dam.
skillTips.inference: "Its job is patience" is not literal. Ask what patience does here, then read the sentence about wet and dry months for the answer.
skillTips.vocabulary: Both "watershed" and "reservoir" are explained in the sentence that names them. When a passage says "is called," the meaning sits right beside it.
skillTips.detail: The watershed is defined once, in one sentence. Find that sentence and match its words instead of picking what sounds close.

passages.title: How Water Is Made Safe
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Water leaving a reservoir is not yet drinkable. It carries clay, leaves, and living things too small to see. Between the reservoir and the tap sits a treatment plant, and its work happens in a fixed order.

First the water is made to drop what it carries. A chemical is stirred in that makes the tiny particles stick to one another in clumps heavy enough to sink. The water then sits still in a wide tank while those clumps settle to the bottom. Stillness does most of the cleaning here, and stillness is free.

Next comes the filter, usually a deep bed of sand and gravel. Water passes down through it and leaves behind whatever the settling missed.

The water is now clear. Clear is not the same as safe. Some bacteria are small enough to pass through sand, so the last step kills them, with chlorine or with ultraviolet light.

Each step is cheap because the step before it did its share. Send raw river water straight to a filter and the filter clogs within an hour.

questions.stem: What is the main point of the passage?
choices: Sand filters are the most important part of cleaning water.
Water taken from a reservoir is dangerous to drink.
A treatment plant cleans water in a fixed order, each step preparing the next.
Chlorine is the cheapest way to make water safe.
questions.explanation: Each paragraph is one step, and the last paragraph explains why the steps cannot be reordered. The order is the point, not any single step.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what makes the tiny particles sink?
choices: A chemical stirred in that makes them clump together.
The weight of the sand and gravel above them.
Chlorine added at the start of the process.
Heat applied to the water in a wide tank.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says a chemical is stirred in that makes the particles stick to one another in clumps heavy enough to sink. Chlorine comes last, and heat is never mentioned.

questions.stem: In this passage, "settle" means
choices: become calm after a disagreement
sink slowly to the bottom and stay there
pay what is owed
spread out evenly across a surface
questions.explanation: The clumps are heavy enough to sink, and they settle while the water sits still in a tank. The everyday senses of the word do not fit what is happening.

questions.stem: Why would a filter clog within an hour if it were fed raw river water?
choices: River water moves too fast for a bed of sand.
Sand and gravel wear out quickly when they are used.
Chlorine has to be added before water can be filtered.
The settling step normally removes most of the material first.
questions.explanation: The passage says each step is cheap because the one before did its share. Without settling, everything that would have sunk arrives at the filter instead.

lesson.strategy: This is a process in a fixed order: settle, filter, disinfect. Read for the order, and for what each step leaves the next one to do. The final paragraph explains why the order cannot be changed, and that is the real point of the passage.

signals.phrase: its work happens in a fixed order
signals.means: Tells you to read the rest as a sequence, and that the sequence itself matters.

signals.phrase: First the water is made to drop what it carries.
signals.means: The opening stage. "First" promises more stages behind it.

signals.phrase: Clear is not the same as safe.
signals.means: A turn. The writer corrects an assumption the sentence before it invited.

signals.phrase: because the step before it did its share
signals.means: The main idea, saved for the end: the steps depend on one another.

vocab.inContext: sink slowly to the bottom of still water
a bed of sand and gravel that traps what the water carries through it
living things too small to see, some of which cause illness

skillTips.main-idea: Every paragraph is one step of the same process. The main idea is the process and its order, not whichever step sounds most impressive.
skillTips.inference: The clogged filter is a thought experiment, not a reported fact. Work backwards to what settling must normally remove.
skillTips.vocabulary: "Settle" is explained by what surrounds it: the water sits still and the clumps go to the bottom. Use the action, not the everyday sense.
skillTips.detail: Each step has its own tool: a chemical, a wide tank, sand, chlorine. Match the question's step to its own sentence before answering.

passages.title: The Push in the Pipe
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Clean water in a tank is still useless. It has to reach a fifth-floor kitchen, and it has to arrive with enough force to fill a glass in seconds. That force is pressure, and a city buys it with height.

The oldest method is the simplest. Pump the treated water up into a tall tank and let gravity do the rest. The higher the tank stands above the taps, the harder the water pushes when a tap is opened. This is why a water tower sits on the highest ground a town owns, or on legs that lift it clear of the roofs.

A tower also buys time. Pumps run at a steady rate, but people do not use water at a steady rate; a city wakes, washes, and cooks inside the same hour. The tank fills through the quiet night and drains through the busy morning, so the pumps never have to be sized for the worst minute of the day. When the power fails, the tower holds the pressure up until it empties.

The same pressure that serves the fifth floor also pushes on every joint in the network. Where a pipe is weak, pressure finds it.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: Height gives a water system its pressure, and that pressure both serves buildings and strains pipes.
Water towers cost less to build than the pumps they replace.
Tall buildings use far more water than short ones.
Pumps should be sized for the busiest minute of the day.
questions.explanation: The passage explains how height makes pressure, lists what the tower buys, then closes by turning that same pressure into a problem. Only the first choice holds both halves.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what does a tower let a city avoid?
choices: Treating the same water twice.
Building anything on high ground.
Sizing its pumps for the worst minute of the day.
Using gravity to move water through pipes.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph says the tank fills at night and drains in the morning, so the pumps never have to be sized for the worst minute of the day.

questions.stem: In this passage, "pressure" is best understood as
choices: the weight of the tank and its legs
the demand people place on a water system
the speed at which the pumps turn
the force that pushes water out of a tap
questions.explanation: Pressure is introduced as the force that fills a glass in seconds, and at the end it is the force pushing on every joint. It is a push, not a weight, a speed, or a demand.

questions.stem: The last two sentences suggest that
choices: the height that makes taps work also makes leaks more likely
water should be shut off at night to rest the pipes
weak pipes should be replaced before any tower is built
a fifth-floor kitchen wastes more water than a ground-floor one
questions.explanation: The passage says the same pressure serves the fifth floor and pushes on every joint, and that pressure finds a weak pipe. The benefit and the risk come from one cause.

lesson.strategy: An engineering passage built on a single idea: height makes pressure. Track the three things the tower buys, which are reach, a steady supply, and a backup. Then notice the turn in the last two sentences, where the same pressure becomes a cost.

signals.phrase: a city buys it with height
signals.means: The central idea in five words. Height is the source of the pressure.

signals.phrase: A tower also buys time.
signals.means: "Also" adds a second use. The tower is not only about reaching upper floors.

signals.phrase: but people do not use water at a steady rate
signals.means: The mismatch the tank exists to absorb: steady supply against uneven demand.

signals.phrase: Where a pipe is weak, pressure finds it.
signals.means: A closing turn. The benefit and the damage come from the same force.

vocab.inContext: the push that sends water out of a tap
the downward pull that makes a raised tank push water outward
the whole connected system of pipes running under a city

skillTips.main-idea: Three paragraphs give three uses of one idea. State the idea to yourself, height makes pressure, before you judge any answer choice.
skillTips.inference: The final line adds no new fact. It reuses one. Ask what pressure does to a weak joint, given everything the passage already said pressure does.
skillTips.vocabulary: "Pressure" is defined by its effects: it fills a glass in seconds and pushes on joints. Read the verbs around a word to fix its meaning.
skillTips.detail: The night-and-morning sentence carries the pump answer. When a question asks what a tower avoids, look for the phrase "never have to be."

passages.title: After the Drain
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Half of a water system runs the other way. Everything that leaves a sink, a shower, or a toilet enters a second network of pipes, sloping downhill toward a plant on the low edge of the city.

What arrives is mostly water. The trouble is what is dissolved in it. Screens and settling tanks take out the solids in the first hour, much as a drinking-water plant does, but they cannot touch what has dissolved.

For that, the plant hires bacteria. Air is blown up through a long tank of wastewater, and a dense population of microbes feeds on the dissolved waste, turning it into more microbes. The plant is not a machine that strips the waste out; it is a place where something is kept alive and fed well. The living sludge is then left to settle, and most of it is pumped back to the head of the tank to keep the population strong.

The water that leaves goes into a river. Somewhere downstream, another city's reservoir is filling. That is the part of the loop nobody sees, and it explains why the standard for what leaves a plant is set by the people who will drink it.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: Sewage pipes have to slope downhill in order to work.
Dissolved waste cannot be removed from water.
Wastewater is cleaned mostly by bacteria and then returned to a river others will drink from.
Cities should build their treatment plants on high ground.
questions.explanation: The passage names the method, which is a fed population of microbes, and then the reason it must work, which is that the water goes downstream to somebody's reservoir.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what can the screens and settling tanks not remove?
choices: Whatever has dissolved in the water.
The solids that sink to the bottom.
The microbes living in the long tank.
The air that is blown through the water.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says they take out the solids but cannot touch what has dissolved. That limit is what forces the next step.

questions.stem: In this passage, material that is "dissolved" is
choices: floating on the surface of the water
resting at the bottom of a settling tank
broken into pieces by a screen
mixed into the water so completely that it cannot be strained out
questions.explanation: The word is defined by what defeats it: screens and settling tanks cannot touch it, so it is not floating, sitting, or catchable.

questions.stem: Why does the passage say the standard is "set by the people who will drink it"?
choices: Cities downstream help pay for the plants upstream.
The river carries the treated water into another city's supply.
Drinking-water plants and sewage plants use the same machines.
Bacteria cannot survive in water that has been made too clean.
questions.explanation: The water leaves into a river, and downstream another city's reservoir is filling. What one plant releases becomes the next city's raw supply.

lesson.strategy: This is the return half of a system you have seen going out. Read it against the drinking-water plant it names: the same screens, the same settling, then one step that is completely different. The final paragraph closes the loop and gives the reason the passage was heading toward.

signals.phrase: runs the other way
signals.means: Frames the whole passage as the reverse of the supply side of the system.

signals.phrase: they cannot touch what has dissolved
signals.means: Names the limit that forces the next step. Expect a new method right after this.

signals.phrase: the plant hires bacteria
signals.means: The turn to the surprising method. "Hires" tells you the microbes do the work.

signals.phrase: another city's reservoir is filling
signals.means: The point of the passage: treated wastewater becomes somebody else's supply.

vocab.inContext: used water leaving homes, carrying whatever was washed or flushed away
living things too small to see, here the ones that eat dissolved waste
further along a river, in the direction the water is flowing

skillTips.main-idea: The passage gives a method and then a reason. A main idea that holds only one of them is incomplete: bacteria clean it, and someone downstream drinks it.
skillTips.inference: The last sentence assumes you remember where a reservoir sits. Connect "goes into a river" to "another city's reservoir" and the reason follows.
skillTips.vocabulary: "Dissolved" is defined by what fails against it. Screens and settling tanks cannot touch it, so let that failure describe the word.
skillTips.detail: The stages are split across paragraphs: screens and tanks first, then the aerated tank. Go back to the right paragraph before choosing.

passages.title: The Cost of a Cheap Glass
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A glass of tap water costs a household a fraction of a cent. That price is honest about the water and dishonest about everything else.

The water itself is free; it falls out of the sky. What a bill pays for is the watershed bought and protected, the reservoir and its dam, the treatment plant, the pumps, the tower, and the buried mains that carry pressure to every street. Almost none of that cost moves with the amount you use. A city that sells ten percent less water does not spend ten percent less. The pipes are just as long, and the plant runs anyway.

This is the awkward arithmetic of a network. The costs are fixed and enormous, the product is cheap and essential, and the customers vote. Raising the price of water is unpopular in a way that raising the price of almost nothing else is, so the price tends to stay where it was while the pipes age underneath it.

The bill for that arrives late, and in another form. In many systems a fifth or more of the treated water never reaches a tap, leaking out of joints laid before anyone now living was working. The cheap glass was never cheap. Its real price was paid in postponement, and postponement charges interest.

questions.stem: What is the central claim of the passage?
choices: Water is expensive to treat because of the chemicals a plant uses.
Leaking pipes are the main reason water bills go up.
Cities should sell more water in order to cover their costs.
A water bill pays for a fixed, aging system, and holding the price down only postpones a larger cost.
questions.explanation: The claim is set in the second sentence and returned to at the end. The leaks and the ten percent are evidence for it, not the claim itself.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what happens to a city's spending when it sells ten percent less water?
choices: It stays much the same, because the costs do not move with use.
It falls by roughly ten percent.
It rises, because the plant has to run longer.
It falls, but only once the old pipes are replaced.
questions.explanation: The passage answers this twice in a row: the pipes are just as long, and the plant runs anyway.

questions.stem: In this passage, costs that are "fixed" are costs that
choices: have already been repaired
are set by law and cannot be altered
stay much the same whether much or little water is sold
are paid once, when the system is first built
questions.explanation: Two sentences earlier the passage says almost none of that cost moves with the amount you use, and gives the ten percent example to prove it.

questions.stem: What does the passage mean by "postponement charges interest"?
choices: Cities have to borrow money in order to replace old pipes.
Interest rates decide when a city can afford new mains.
Water bills rise by a small amount every year.
Putting off repairs makes the eventual cost larger.
questions.explanation: The image is borrowed from lending: a debt left unpaid grows. Here the debt is maintenance, and the growth shows up as a fifth of the treated water leaking away.

lesson.strategy: An argument, not an explanation. The claim sits in the second sentence, and everything after it is support: what the bill actually buys, why the price will not rise, and what the delay costs. Read the last line as the claim restated.

signals.phrase: honest about the water and dishonest about everything else
signals.means: The thesis in one line. The rest of the passage unpacks the dishonest half.

signals.phrase: This is the awkward arithmetic of a network.
signals.means: A summary sentence. The three clauses after it compress the whole argument.

signals.phrase: so the price tends to stay where it was
signals.means: The consequence. Politics, not cost, is what holds the price still.

signals.phrase: postponement charges interest
signals.means: A metaphor from lending: a delayed repair grows more expensive, like a debt.

vocab.inContext: the large buried pipes that carry water beneath the streets
not changing with how much is used or sold
putting off something that will still have to be done

skillTips.main-idea: In an argument the main idea is the claim, not the evidence. The leaks and the ten percent are there to support a claim about price.
skillTips.inference: "Postponement charges interest" borrows a word from lending. Ask what an unpaid debt does over time, then apply that to an unrepaired pipe.
skillTips.vocabulary: "Fixed" is defined two sentences before it appears, in plain words: the cost does not move with the amount you use. Look before a word as well as after it.
skillTips.detail: The ten percent sentence answers directly and then answers again: the pipes are just as long, the plant runs anyway.

passages.title: Why Onions Make You Cry
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
An onion on the table is quiet. Cut it, and your eyes sting within seconds. The onion is not doing this to you. It is defending itself, and you are standing too close.

Inside an onion, two things are kept apart in separate rooms. One is a chemical the plant has stored. The other is a tool that changes it. A knife breaks the walls between them. They meet, and the onion makes a new gas that rises into the air.

The gas reaches your eye. There it meets the thin layer of water on the surface and turns into a weak acid. Your eye feels the sting and does the only thing it can. It makes tears to wash the acid away.

This is why a sharp knife helps. It cuts the cells instead of crushing them, so less gas escapes. A cold onion helps too. Cold slows the whole reaction down.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: How onions grow and store their food.
Why cutting an onion makes a gas that stings the eyes.
Why some knives cut better than others.
How tears protect the body from harm.
questions.explanation: The passage follows one chain from the knife to the tears. The knife and the tears are steps in that chain, not the subject.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what happens when a knife breaks the walls inside an onion?
choices: Two things that were kept apart meet and make a gas.
Water leaks out onto the surface of the eye.
The onion begins to dry out.
The onion turns colder.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says the two were kept apart in separate rooms, the knife breaks the walls, and then they meet and make a new gas.

questions.stem: In this passage, a "reaction" is
choices: a strong feeling about a smell
a tool used for cutting food
the way an eye moves when it stings
a change that happens when two things meet
questions.explanation: The passage has already shown two things meeting and making something new. When cold "slows the whole reaction down," the reaction is that change.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that how much your eyes sting depends on
choices: how large the onion is
how much gas escapes from the cut onion
how long the onion has been stored
how close your face is to the table
questions.explanation: A sharp knife lets less gas escape and it helps. Turn that around: more gas means more sting. Size, storage, and the table are never mentioned.

lesson.strategy: A chain of causes in four steps: a cut, a gas, an acid, tears. Take one sentence at a time and ask what it causes next. The last paragraph turns the chain into two pieces of advice, and the advice only makes sense if you followed the chain.

signals.phrase: It is defending itself
signals.means: Frames the sting as the onion's purpose, not an accident.

signals.phrase: They meet, and the onion makes a new gas
signals.means: The turning point. Nothing stings until these two things meet.

signals.phrase: turns into a weak acid
signals.means: The step that explains the pain. The gas by itself is not what hurts.

signals.phrase: This is why a sharp knife helps.
signals.means: A move from explanation to advice. The reason follows straight after.

vocab.inContext: something like air that spreads out and cannot be seen
something that stings or burns what it touches
the tiny rooms a living thing is built from

skillTips.main-idea: Each paragraph is one link in the same chain, from the knife to the tears. Choose the answer that covers the chain, not one link in it.
skillTips.inference: The passage never says "more gas means more sting." It says a sharp knife makes less gas and helps. Turn that around to get the rule.
skillTips.vocabulary: "Acid" is explained by what happens next: the eye stings and makes tears to wash it away. Let the effect tell you the meaning.
skillTips.detail: The two things inside the onion are described before they are named. Reread the second paragraph slowly before you answer about the knife.

passages.title: How a Zipper Holds
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
A zipper looks like one thing. It is really three: two rows of teeth, and a small slider that runs between them.

Look closely at a single tooth. On its top there is a little bump. On its bottom there is a small hollow. Every tooth is the same shape, and the two rows face each other.

Now the slider. Inside it, the path splits into a Y. When you pull the slider up, the two rows come in through the wide end and are forced together at an angle. The bump on one tooth drops into the hollow of the tooth opposite. Once it is seated, that tooth cannot lift out unless it is bent sideways again, and the teeth beside it hold it flat.

Pull the slider the other way and a small wedge inside it slides between the rows and lifts them apart. The slider does no gripping of its own. The teeth hold each other.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: Why zippers are better than buttons.
How a slider is made in a factory.
How the teeth of a zipper lock into each other as the slider passes.
Why zippers sometimes break and stick.
questions.explanation: The passage describes one tooth, then the slider, then what happens when it moves each way. All of it explains the locking.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what is on the bottom of each tooth?
choices: A small hollow.
A little bump.
A small wedge.
A row of stitches.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph gives both: the bump is on the top, the hollow is on the bottom.

questions.stem: In this passage, a "wedge" is
choices: a handle you hold with your fingers
a piece that joins two things together
a row of metal teeth
a shape that pushes things apart as it moves between them
questions.explanation: The last paragraph says the wedge slides between the rows and lifts them apart. That is what it does, so that is what it is.

questions.stem: The last two sentences suggest that a zipper stays closed because
choices: each tooth is held in place by the teeth beside it
the slider grips the two rows tightly
the cloth pulls the two rows together
the teeth are made of very hard metal
questions.explanation: The slider does no gripping, so it is not holding anything. The passage has already said the teeth beside a seated tooth hold it flat.

lesson.strategy: A description of a small machine. Read it in the order it gives you: one tooth, then the slider, then the two directions of travel. Picture each part before moving on. The last two sentences say where the strength really comes from.

signals.phrase: It is really three
signals.means: Warns you that the obvious view is wrong, and sets up the three parts.

signals.phrase: the path splits into a Y
signals.means: The key shape. The Y is what forces the two rows together.

signals.phrase: Once it is seated
signals.means: The moment of locking. Everything before this was preparation.

signals.phrase: The teeth hold each other.
signals.means: The main idea in four words, saved for the last line.

vocab.inContext: the small piece you pull, which joins or parts the two rows
a small dip that another shape fits into
a shape that widens toward one end and pushes things apart

skillTips.main-idea: The passage explains how a thing works. Its main idea is how the parts act on each other, not what a zipper is used for.
skillTips.inference: The closing lines say the slider does no gripping. If it is not holding the zipper shut, ask what is, and only one part is left.
skillTips.vocabulary: "Wedge" is described by its job in the same sentence: it slides between the rows and lifts them apart.
skillTips.detail: The top and the bottom of a tooth are given in two short sentences. Check which one the question asks about before you answer.

passages.title: Why Names Slip Away
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
You meet someone, talk for ten minutes, and remember that she is a nurse, that she has just moved here, and that she laughs easily. Her name is gone. This happens to almost everyone, and it is not a sign of a poor memory.

Memory holds on to things that connect to other things. A job is full of connections. Hearing "nurse" brings up a hospital, a uniform, a night shift, someone you already know. The word has somewhere to attach.

A name has nowhere. Nothing about a woman called Rose is rose-like. The sound is a label, chosen before she was born, and it links to nothing else you know about her. So it sits alone, and things that sit alone are the first to go.

There is a second reason, and it is simpler. In the moment of meeting, most people are busy deciding what to say next. The name is spoken while you are not listening.

questions.stem: What is the main idea of the passage?
choices: Most people have a poor memory for faces.
It is rude to forget a person's name.
Names are hard to remember because they connect to nothing else we know.
A person's job is the easiest thing to remember about them.
questions.explanation: The passage compares a job, which has many connections, with a name, which has none. That contrast is the whole explanation.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what does hearing the word "nurse" bring up?
choices: A hospital, a uniform, a night shift, someone you already know.
A face you cannot quite place.
A name you have heard somewhere before.
A feeling of being busy and tired.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph lists exactly these four things as what the word attaches to.

questions.stem: In this passage, a "label" is
choices: a small sticker put on a bottle
a name given to something that says nothing about it
a short description of a person's work
a word that is easy to say out loud
questions.explanation: The sentence says the sound was chosen before she was born and links to nothing else about her. A label names without describing.

questions.stem: The passage suggests that you would remember a name better if
choices: you met the person in a quieter room
the person had an unusual job
it connected to something you already knew
you heard it spoken more loudly
questions.explanation: The rule is that memory holds what connects. Names fail because they connect to nothing, so a name with a connection would hold better.

lesson.strategy: Two reasons for one everyday problem. The first takes three paragraphs and rests on a comparison between a job and a name. The second gets four lines. Watch for the sentence that announces the second reason, or you will read straight past it.

signals.phrase: it is not a sign of a poor memory
signals.means: Clears away the obvious explanation before the real one arrives.

signals.phrase: Memory holds on to things that connect to other things.
signals.means: The rule the passage rests on. Everything after it tests names against this rule.

signals.phrase: A name has nowhere.
signals.means: The comparison snaps shut. The job had connections; the name has none.

signals.phrase: There is a second reason
signals.means: A plain marker that a new cause is being added, not the old one repeated.

vocab.inContext: join on to something else you already know
hold on to something, so it has a place to stay
a name put on something that does not describe it

skillTips.main-idea: Two reasons are given, but only one is developed at length. The main idea is the connection rule, with the second reason as an addition.
skillTips.inference: The passage explains why names fail to stick. Reverse that explanation to see what would make one stick instead.
skillTips.vocabulary: "Label" is explained by the words around it: chosen before she was born, linked to nothing about her.
skillTips.detail: The list after "nurse" has four items. Match all of them, not just the first one you recognize.

passages.title: The First Street Lights
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
For most of history, a city went dark at sunset. Anyone who had to go out carried a lantern, or paid a boy with a torch to walk in front of them. Some towns ordered every household to hang a lamp by its door on winter nights. The light was thin, and it ended where the house ended.

In January 1807, a street in London called Pall Mall was lit with gas. Pipes ran under the pavement, and a small flame burned at the top of each post. The light was steady, and it did not blow out. Within twenty years, gas lamps stood in cities across Europe and America.

Someone still had to walk those streets each evening with a ladder and a flame. Lamplighters had a route and a time, and people set their evenings by them. Electricity ended that work. A whole street could be lit from one switch, by a person who never left the room.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: How city streets went from carried lanterns to gas lamps and then to electric light.
Why gas lamps were dangerous in cold weather.
How London grew larger after 1807.
Why people stopped going out after dark.
questions.explanation: Each paragraph is one stage of the same change, and the last one closes it with electricity.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what did some towns order every household to do?
choices: Hang a lamp by its door on winter nights.
Pay a boy to carry a torch through the street.
Keep a candle burning until sunrise.
Stay indoors after the sun went down.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph states the rule directly. Paying a boy with a torch was a private choice, not an order.

questions.stem: In this passage, a "lantern" is
choices: a lamp fixed to the top of a post
a light you carry, with the flame held inside a case
a pipe that brings gas under a street
a ladder used to reach a high lamp
questions.explanation: It is what a person carried when going out at night, before any street had lamps of its own.

questions.stem: Why did electricity end the lamplighter's work?
choices: Cities had grown too large for anyone to walk across.
Gas pipes were dug up and taken away.
Electric lamps were cheaper to buy than gas lamps.
One switch could light a whole street, so nobody had to walk it.
questions.explanation: The last sentence describes a person who never left the room lighting a whole street. If nobody walks the route, the job is gone.

lesson.strategy: A short history in three stages: carried light, gas light, electric light. Each paragraph is one stage, and each stage removes something the stage before it needed. Read for what disappears, not only for what arrives.

signals.phrase: For most of history, a city went dark at sunset.
signals.means: Sets the starting condition. Everything after this is a change away from it.

signals.phrase: In January 1807
signals.means: A date marks the turn. The first stage has ended and the second begins.

signals.phrase: Someone still had to walk those streets
signals.means: "Still" signals that the change was not complete. A limit is coming.

signals.phrase: Electricity ended that work.
signals.means: The final stage, stated as a loss as much as a gain.

vocab.inContext: a light you carry, with the flame inside a case
the hard walking path at the side of a street
a fixed path that someone follows each time

skillTips.main-idea: Three stages, one subject. Choose the answer that names the change across all three, not the one that stops at gas.
skillTips.inference: The last two sentences give a cause without using the word "because." Put the one switch and the person who never left the room together.
skillTips.vocabulary: "Lantern" sits next to people who had to go out at night. What they carried tells you what it is.
skillTips.detail: The household rule is in the first paragraph and the lamplighters are in the third. Go back to the right paragraph before choosing.

passages.title: The Farmer Who Photographed Snow
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Wilson Bentley was a farmer in Vermont. He was also the first person to photograph a single snow crystal.

He was fifteen when his mother gave him an old microscope. He caught snowflakes on a black board, carried them into a cold shed, and looked. What he saw would melt in a minute, and he could not draw fast enough. So he asked for a camera, and his family bought one that cost more than the farm could easily spare.

It took him two winters to get one picture. He was nineteen. He kept going for forty-six more years, in a shed with no heat, working in the cold so that his subject would not vanish. He made more than five thousand photographs of snow crystals.

He never sold many. He gave prints away and charged little, and in his village he was known mostly as a strange, patient neighbor. The pictures outlasted the opinion. Almost every image of a snowflake we know began in that shed.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: Snow crystals melt too quickly to be studied properly.
A Vermont farmer spent his life photographing snow crystals.
Cameras were rare and costly on farms in the 1800s.
A microscope is the best tool for studying snow.
questions.explanation: The passage is about one man and one long task. The camera and the microscope are tools in that story.

questions.stem: According to the passage, how long did it take Bentley to get his first picture?
choices: Two winters.
Forty-six years.
Fifteen years.
A single night.
questions.explanation: The third paragraph opens with it. Forty-six years is how long he worked afterward, and fifteen is his age when he got the microscope.

questions.stem: In this passage, "patient" describes someone who
choices: is waiting to be seen by a doctor
is gentle and quiet with other people
works quickly but very carefully
keeps working at something slow without giving up
questions.explanation: Two winters for one picture, then forty-six years in an unheated shed. The numbers around the word show what it means here.

questions.stem: "The pictures outlasted the opinion" suggests that
choices: photographs last longer than snow does
he became famous while he was still alive
what his village thought of him mattered less in the end than his work
he changed his neighbors' minds about him
questions.explanation: The opinion is the village calling him strange. The pictures are still with us, so the work outlived the judgement.

lesson.strategy: A life told through one stubborn task. Watch the numbers: fifteen, two winters, nineteen, forty-six years, five thousand. They carry a point the sentences never state outright. The last line puts the value of the work outside his lifetime.

signals.phrase: the first person to photograph a single snow crystal
signals.means: The claim the passage supports. Read everything after it as how he did it.

signals.phrase: It took him two winters to get one picture.
signals.means: The cost of the work, given as a plain fact. Expect more numbers like it.

signals.phrase: He never sold many.
signals.means: A turn from what he achieved to how little it was valued at the time.

signals.phrase: The pictures outlasted the opinion.
signals.means: The closing judgement, weighing his work against what his village thought.

vocab.inContext: a solid with a regular shape, here one piece of snow
a tool that makes very small things look large
willing to keep going slowly, without hurrying or quitting

skillTips.main-idea: This is about a person and one task. A main idea has to join them: who he was and what he spent his life doing.
skillTips.inference: The last paragraph never says he was ignored. It says he charged little and was thought strange. Read the tone as well as the facts.
skillTips.vocabulary: "Patient" is proved by the numbers near it: two winters, forty-six years, a shed with no heat.
skillTips.detail: The numbers are easy to mix up. Two winters is the first picture; forty-six years is everything that came after.

passages.title: Why Passwords Got Longer
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
Twenty years ago, a good password was short and strange. The advice then asked for a capital letter, a number, and a symbol, and eight characters was enough. That advice has changed, and the reason is arithmetic.

A password is only as strong as the number of guesses needed to find it. Machines do the guessing now, and they do it in parallel, millions of tries a second against a stolen file. Under that kind of attack, eight characters fall in hours, whatever symbols are hidden in them.

Adding one more character does far more than adding one more symbol. Each new character multiplies the number of possible passwords by the size of the alphabet. Length compounds; complexity does not.

There is a second change, and it is not about math. People could not remember the short strange passwords, so they used the same one everywhere. When a single site is broken into, every account sharing that password opens at once. So the advice now is a long phrase of three or four words nobody else would put together, a different one per account, kept in a password manager or written somewhere safe.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: Symbols make passwords too difficult to type.
People should change their passwords more often than they do.
Password advice changed because length resists fast guessing better than symbols do.
Stolen files are the greatest danger a website faces.
questions.explanation: The passage states that the advice changed, then gives the arithmetic reason and the human one. Length against complexity is the core of it.

questions.stem: According to the passage, how long does an eight-character password last under attack?
choices: Seconds.
Hours.
Several weeks.
It depends on which symbols are in it.
questions.explanation: The second paragraph says eight characters fall in hours, and adds "whatever symbols are hidden in them," which rules out the last choice.

questions.stem: In this passage, "complexity" refers to
choices: the odd mix of capitals, numbers, and symbols in a password
the number of accounts one person has to manage
how hard a password is to type correctly
the strength that comes from extra length
questions.explanation: Complexity is set against length in the same sentence, so it must mean the other thing the old advice asked for: capitals, numbers, and symbols.

questions.stem: Why does using the same password everywhere matter so much?
choices: Machines can guess a reused password more quickly.
Long passwords are harder to reuse than short ones.
Websites are broken into less often than they used to be.
One broken site opens every account that shares that password.
questions.explanation: The passage states the mechanism directly: when one site is broken into, every account sharing that password opens at once.

lesson.strategy: An argument that the old advice was wrong. It offers two reasons, one about arithmetic and one about people. Find the sentence where the second begins. The last line turns the argument into a rule, so check that the rule follows from both reasons.

signals.phrase: the reason is arithmetic
signals.means: Promises a numerical argument rather than an opinion. The next paragraph delivers it.

signals.phrase: Length compounds; complexity does not.
signals.means: The claim in four words. The semicolon sets the two ideas directly against each other.

signals.phrase: There is a second change
signals.means: A clean break. The passage moves from arithmetic to human behavior.

signals.phrase: opens at once
signals.means: The cost of reuse, compressed into three words. One break becomes many.

vocab.inContext: the single letters, numbers, or symbols a password is made of
many at the same time, rather than one after another
grows by multiplying, so each step adds more than the last one did

skillTips.main-idea: Two reasons support one claim, that the advice changed. Do not pick an answer that states only one of the reasons.
skillTips.inference: The reuse paragraph never uses the word risk. It describes one break opening many accounts, and you name the risk yourself.
skillTips.vocabulary: "Compounds" is explained by the sentence before it: each character multiplies the possibilities. Read the example, then the word.
skillTips.detail: The numbers here are exact: eight characters, hours, millions a second. Match the one the question actually asks for.

passages.title: Your Name in a Loud Room
passages.attribution: Original passage © Studio AM, written for Fluency.
passages.text:
At a crowded party you can follow one voice and let the rest of the room become noise. It feels like closing a door. Then someone across the room says your name, and you hear it.

Both of those are true, and together they say something odd about attention. If the door were really shut, your name could not get through. If it were open, you would be flooded.

A researcher named Colin Cherry tested this in the 1950s. He played two different recordings, one into each ear, and asked people to repeat one of them aloud as it went. They managed it. Afterwards they could report almost nothing about the ignored ear: not the topic, not the words. But in a later study built on his method, about a third of listeners noticed their own name when it was slipped into the ear they were ignoring.

So the ignored channel is not switched off. Something keeps reading all of it, cheaply and without your knowledge, and interrupts you when it finds something that matters.

questions.stem: What is the passage mainly about?
choices: People are unable to follow two conversations at the same time.
The sound you are ignoring is still being checked for things that matter.
Crowded parties are difficult places to hold a conversation.
Hearing works better than sight in a noisy room.
questions.explanation: The passage sets up a puzzle, uses the study as evidence, and answers it in the last paragraph: something keeps reading the ignored side.

questions.stem: According to the passage, what could Cherry's listeners report about the ignored ear?
choices: The topic, but not the exact words.
Their own name, and nothing else.
Almost nothing: not the topic and not the words.
Everything they had heard on that side.
questions.explanation: The passage says they could report almost nothing, and then names both things they missed. The name result came from a later study.
